Achilles.note: Nine Muses lament Achilles in alternating voices for seventeen days.
Nereus is Achilles' maternal grandfather through Thetis.
The Nereids join Thetis in mourning Achilles.
Poseidon intervenes against Achilles to remove the endangered Aeneas.
Immersion in Styx is presented as the source of Achilles’ protection.
Achilles is the mortal son of Thetis and Peleus.
She tells Achilles he may choose long obscurity or brief imperishable fame.
She obtains Hephaestus-made armor and delivers it to her grieving son.
Thetis burns away Achilles’ mortality with fire and ambrosia until Peleus interrupts.
Thetis dips Achilles in the Styx in the earliest extant immersion account.
After his death, Thetis removes Achilles from the pyre to Leuke.
Zeus grants Trojan success to honor Achilles after Thetis supplicates him.
Zeus weighs the fates of Achilles and Hector before their confrontation.

Acis.note: Jealous of Galatea's love, Polyphemus crushes Acis beneath a rock.
Some late variants assign Acis to Pan as his offspring.

Acis.myth: Polyphemus crushes Acis with a rock
Acis.note: Jealous of Galatea’s lover, Polyphemus kills Acis, who becomes a river-god.

Acmon.note: A doubtful lexicographical notice may call Charon an Akmonidēs, son of Acmon.

Actaeon.note: Artemis transforms Actaeon into a stag after he sees her bathing.
After Artemis transforms him, Actaeon is torn apart by his dogs.
Fragmentary and later traditions plausibly include Actaeon among Chiron's fosterlings or pupils.

Actis.note: Actis is listed among Helios's Rhodian sons.

Admete.note: Admete is an Oceanid daughter of Tethys and Oceanus.

Admetus.note: Artemis fills Admetus’ marriage chamber with snakes after he neglects her sacrifice.
The Fates permit another person to die in Admetus' place.

Adrasteia.note: Damascius presents Adrasteia as an alternative name or equation for Ananke.
Philosophical allegory treats both names as aspects of invincible causal order.
Adrasteia, identified with Ananke, is closely coupled beside Chronos.
Nemesis and Adrasteia received joint worship at Andros and Cos.
Later tradition merged Adrasteia’s functions and identity with Nemesis.
Adrasteia guards Nyx's cave and clashes cymbals while Zeus is reared.
Rhea entrusts infant Zeus to the nymph Adrasteia.

Aeacus.note: Aeacus is honored beside Plouton and entrusted with the underworld keys.

Aeetes.note: Aeetes possesses armor given by Ares after the god killed Mimas.
Aeetes, king of Colchis, is a son of Helios and Perse.
Aeetes is Pasiphae's brother in the standard solar genealogy.

Aegialeus.note: Diodorus makes Aegialeus Circe’s brother through Hecate and Aeëtes.

Aegipan.note: Aegipan cooperates with Hermes to recover and restore Zeus's sinews.

Aegle.note: A classical variant makes Aegle mother of the Charites.
A local or late genealogy pairs Aegle with Helios.
Aegle laments beside Ladon’s corpse and recounts Heracles’ attack.

Aeneas.note: At Juno's request, Aeolus unleashes winds against Aeneas' Trojan fleet.
Aeneas is Aphrodite's son by Anchises.
Aphrodite shields Aeneas from Diomedes and is wounded while rescuing him.
Apollo protects and rescues Aeneas during battle.
Aeneas passes Cerberus after the Sibyl drugs the guardian with a honey-cake.
After initially refusing Aeneas, Charon accepts the golden bough and ferries him.
The Cyclopes forge the divinely commissioned armor carried by Aeneas.
Aphrodite says mountain nymphs will rear her son Aeneas.

Aeneas.myth: Aeneas escapes the blinded Cyclops coast
Aeneas.note: Aeneas’s Trojans encounter the wounded Polyphemus and flee his gathering kin.
Poseidon saves Aeneas because fate requires continuation of Dardanus’ lineage.

Aerope.note: Arcadian local myth makes Aerope the mother by Ares of Aeropus.

Aeropus.note: Aeropus is Ares’s son by Aerope in Arcadian local myth.

Aesepus.note: Aesepus is a river son of Tethys and Oceanus.

Aethra.note: Later genealogical traditions substitute Aethra for Pleione as mother of Atlas's daughters.

Aethra.myth: Latin genealogy of the celestial children
Aethra.note: Hyginus makes Aethra Hyperion’s partner and mother of Sol, Luna, and Aurora.
Poseidon sleeps with Aethra in the tradition giving Theseus divine and mortal fathers.

Aetna.note: A Sicilian genealogy pairs Hephaestus with Aetna as parents of the Palici.

Aetnaeus.note: The Cabeiric Prometheus is father of Aetnaeus.
Prometheus and his son jointly receive Demeter's secret deposit or rite.

Aeëtes.note: Aeëtes is Circe’s brother in Homeric and Hesiodic genealogy.
Aeëtes recalls accompanying Helios when Circe was transported west.
Diodorus alternatively makes Aeëtes Circe’s father by Hecate.

Africus.note: Aeolus releases Africus to help raise the storm against Aeneas.

Agares.note: Modern occult websites equate Agares with Argus without historical evidence.

Agathos Daimon.note: Agathos Daimon was worshipped with or near Tyche at Lebadeia.

Agathyrnus.note: Agathyrnus is one of Aeolus' six colonizing sons.

Agave.note: Harmonia is the mother of Agave.

Agenor.note: Tzetzes names Agenor among Aeolus' twelve intermarried children.
Pseudo-Apollodorus places Argus within Agenor’s Argive royal line.
The standard later synthesis makes Europa a daughter of Agenor.

Aglaea.note: Aglaea, youngest of the Charites, is named as Hephaestus's wife.

Aglauros.note: Aglauros is named as Alcippe’s mother by Ares.

Aglauros.myth: Aglauros blocks Mercury's access to Herse
Aglauros.note: Mercury punishes Aglauros for enviously obstructing his approach to Herse.
Mercury transforms Aglauros into stone after she blocks his way.

Agrius.note: The Moirai collectively kill the Giant Agrius with bronze clubs.
Agrius is named as a son of Circe and Odysseus.
Clotho and the Moirai kill the Giant Agrius with bronze clubs.
The collective Moirai kill the Giant Agrius with bronze clubs.

Aiakos.note: Aiakos is listed among Zeus’s major heroic offspring.

Aidos.note: Aidos and Nemesis veil themselves and leave humanity for Olympus.

Aigaion.note: Pontus and Gaia produce the sea-dwelling ally of the Titans.
Aigaion.date: late seventh century BCE or later

Aigina.note: Aigina is listed among Zeus’s important mortal or semi-divine partners.

Aigipan.note: Aigipan helps recover Zeus’s severed sinews in a later Typhon variant.

Aigle.note: Aigle is named as Asclepius' daughter, embodying healthy radiance.

Aion.note: Aion is frequently identified or functionally overlapped with Chronos in late cosmology.
Aion complains to Zeus that Enyo continually harvests the world's young men.
Modern scholars interpret the disputed Modena figure as Phanes-Aion or an Aionic syncretism.
The ascending ritualist passes Aionic powers before encountering Helios.
Notus and Eurus draw the divine chariot constructed by Aion.

Ajax.note: Athena deludes Ajax after his attempted revenge and displays him to Odysseus.

Ajax the Lesser.note: Athena punishes the returning Greeks because Ajax violated Cassandra at her sanctuary.

Akasha.note: Theosophical writers equate higher Aether with Sanskrit akasha.

Akmon.note: Fragmentary lyric and learned traditions call Uranus the son of Akmon.

Alagonia.note: A poorly attested local genealogy makes Alagonia Europa’s eponymous daughter.

Alcestis.note: Alcestis fulfills the Fates' substitution condition by dying for Admetus.

Alcippe.note: Alcippe is the daughter of Ares and Aglauros.

Alcyone.note: Alcyone is listed as a daughter of Aeolus.
Aeolus restrains the winds for his transformed daughter and Ceyx.
Alcyone is one of Atlas and Pleione's seven daughters.
Alcyone is named as Glaucus' sea-associated mother.

Alcyonides.note: Amphitrite pities Alcyoneus’s drowned daughters and transforms them into halcyon birds.

Alexiares.note: Hebe and Heracles are named as Alexiares' parents.
Later genealogies name Alexiares as Heracles’ son by Hebe.

Algea.note: Eris bears the collective Algea without a named father.

Alilat.note: Herodotus interprets Alilat through a Greek Aphrodite identification.

Alkmene.note: Zeus assumes Amphitryon’s appearance and extends the night to conceive Herakles.

All Olympian gods.note: The Olympian gods receive the infant Pan and delight in him.

Aloadae.note: Ovid and Hyginus transfer the Aloadae’s mountain-piling assault to the Gigantes.

Aloeus.note: Later catalogues attribute Aloeus to Helios.

Alpheus.note: The nymph Arethusa becomes or travels as a spring while fleeing Alpheus.
Alpheus is named among Oceanus's river sons.
Alpheus is a river son of Tethys and Oceanus.

Althaea.note: Althaea hears the Fates' declaration, hides the brand, and later burns it.

Amalthea.note: Amalthea helps rear Zeus within Nyx's cave.
Rhea arranges for Amalthea, goat or nymph, to nurse Zeus.
Hyginus lists Themis alongside Amalthea among possible nurses of Zeus.
Tyche carries Amalthea’s horn in images at Smyrna and Aegeira.

Amaltheia.note: Later Cretan tradition makes Amaltheia nourish the hidden infant Zeus.

Amazons.note: Pegasus carries Bellerophon in his aerial campaign against the Amazons.

Ammon.note: Ammon replaces Zeus as Dionysus’s father in a marginal genealogy.
Ammon is Pasiphae's son by Zeus in one Thalamian genealogy.
Ammon and Themis are invoked together in a Greco-Egyptian detection spell.

Ampelus.myth: Ate tricks Ampelus into riding a bull
Ampelus.note: Disguised as his companion, Ate exploits Ampelus’s insecurity and persuades him to ride a bull.
Ate’s deception causes Ampelus to mount a bull, fall, and die.

Amphiaraus.myth: War of the Seven against Thebes
Amphiaraus.note: Atropos overwhelms Amphiaraus's reluctance and drives him toward his ordained death.
Oneiros appears in imagery associated with Amphiaraus’s incubation oracle.

Amphillogiai.note: Eris bears the collective Amphillogiai without a named father.

Amphimarus.note: Amphimarus fathers Linus with Urania; no courtship or marriage is narrated.

Amphion.note: Amphion is Zeus’s heroic son by Antiope.

Amycus.note: Polydeuces accepts Amycus's compulsory challenge and kills him after the boxing contest.
In alternative accounts Polydeuces defeats Amycus, then binds and spares him.

Amymone.note: Poseidon drives away the satyr attacking Amymone.
Poseidon has intercourse with Amymone and reveals or creates a spring.

Ananke/Necessity.note: The cosmic Sirens revolve upon the eight whorls of her spindle.

Anaxis.note: Anaxis is represented at Argos as a son of the twins.

Anchiale.note: Iapetus fathers Anchiale in a Cilician foundation genealogy.

Anchises.note: Disguised as a Phrygian princess, Aphrodite seduces Anchises.
Aphrodite conceals her divinity from Anchises until after intercourse.

Androcles.note: Androcles is one of Aeolus' six colonizing sons.

Androgeus.note: Androgeus is commonly listed as Ariadne’s brother.

Androktasiai.note: Eris bears the collective Androktasiai without a named father.

Andromache.note: Thetis foretells Andromache’s future and the Molossian succession.

Angelos.note: Scholars probably identify the Sicilian underworld goddess Angelos with Hecate.

Anicetus.note: Hebe and Heracles are named as Anicetus' parents.
Later genealogies name Anicetus as Heracles’ son by Hebe.

Antaeus.note: Gaia is usually the mother of Antaeus by Poseidon.
Gaia repeatedly renews Antaeus’s strength whenever he touches the earth.
Heracles lifts the earth-born wrestler away from Gaia and crushes him.
Later genealogies make Antaeus a son of Poseidon and Gaia.

Anteias.note: Anteias is a son of Circe and Odysseus and eponymous founder of Antium.

Anteros.note: Some later traditions assign Anteros to Aphrodite as a son.

Anteros.myth: Companion who enables Eros to grow
Anteros.note: Aphrodite produces Anteros as reciprocal love and a companion for Eros.

Anthedon.note: The city-eponym Anthedon is named as Glaucus' father.

Antiope.note: Antiope is assigned to Ares among the Amazon queens.
Antiope is listed among Zeus’s important partners.

Aortes.note: Aortes is one of the junior Cyclopes born to the immortal seniors.

Apate.note: Apate and Atropos are siblings under Hesiod's Night genealogy.
Apate and the Keres belong to Nyx's genealogical brood.
Hesiod makes Apate and Momus fatherless children of Nyx.
Apate and Nemesis are fatherless children of Nyx.
Nyx bears Apate without a partner.
Apate and Thanatos belong to Nyx's fatherless brood.

Aphaia.note: Aeginetan Artemis was related to Aphaia, though direct equation is uncertain.

Aphrodite Ambologera.note: Her Spartan image stood near images of Thanatos and Hypnos.

Aphrodite Ourania.note: An Athenian inscription exceptionally calls Aphrodite the eldest of the Moirai.

Aphrodite Pandemos.note: Pausanias's speech assigns Common Aphrodite her corresponding form of Eros.

Aphrodite Urania.note: Pausanias's speech assigns Heavenly Aphrodite her corresponding form of Eros.
An Athenian inscription calls Aphrodite Urania the eldest of the Moirai.

Aquilo.note: Roman writers equate Boreas with the Latin north or northeast wind Aquilo.

Arachne.note: Minerva competes with Arachne, whose tapestry is technically faultless.
Minerva destroys Arachne’s tapestry and strikes her.
After Arachne attempts suicide, Minerva transforms her into a spider.

Aratus.note: Aratus is named as Asclepius' son in a local genealogy.

Ardalus.note: Pausanias calls the Troezenian flute inventor Ardalus a son of Hephaestus.

Ardeias.note: Ardeias is a son of Circe and Odysseus and eponymous founder of Ardea.

Ardescus.note: Ardescus is a river son of Tethys and Oceanus.

Areion.note: The Thelpusan tradition makes divine horse Areion Demeter’s son by Poseidon.

Arensnuphis.note: Local Nubian-Egyptian interpretation associated Heracles with Arensnuphis.

Arestor.note: One genealogical tradition names Argus as Arestor’s son.

Arete.note: Arete teaches that labor and self-command lead to genuine honor.

Arethusa.note: Ovid’s nymph Arethusa informs Ceres about the abducted Proserpina.

Argiope.note: Hyginus names Argiope as Europa’s mother.

Argo.note: The divine speaking ship directs Jason and Medea to Circe for purification.

Argonauts.note: Glaucus advises the Argonauts not to oppose Zeus' plan.
Glaucus accompanies the Argonauts, prophesies, and directs their religious obligations.

Argus.note: Cercops reportedly makes the eponymous Argus a parent of Panoptes.
Hera appoints many-eyed Argus to guard Io.
Juno places dead Argus's eyes in the peacock's tail.

Arion.note: Late epic variants make Zephyrus and an unnamed Harpy Arion’s parents.
An unnamed Harpy bears the supernatural horse Arion to Zephyrus.
Poseidon fathers the divine horse Arion with Demeter.
Some later traditions make Arion the offspring of Zephyrus and a Harpy.

Aristaeus.note: Aristaeus is normally Apollo and Cyrene's son but is included among Chiron's pupils.
Some late lists call Aristaeus Chiron's son, apparently conflating fosterage with descent.
Pherecydes names Aristaeus, son of Paion, as Hecate's father.
Nymphs rear Aristaeus in regional divine-nurse traditions.
Aristaeus binds Proteus and holds him through successive transformations.
Proteus reveals that Eurydice’s death and the nymphs’ anger caused Aristaeus’ bee plague.

Arkas.note: Arkas is Zeus’s son by Kallisto in the dominant genealogy.

Arke.note: Arke is Iris’s winged sister and the Titans’ opposing messenger.

Arne.note: Arne, also called Melanippe, bears Aeolus to Poseidon.
The nymph Arne helps conceal and rear infant Poseidon.

Artemis Stymphalia.myth: Bird imagery at Artemis's Stymphalian sanctuary
Artemis Stymphalia.note: Bird figures and bird-legged maidens decorate her sanctuary, without a narrated encounter.

Artumes.note: The Etruscan goddess was identified iconographically and mythologically with Artemis.

Ascalabus.note: Demeter transforms Ascalabus into a spotted lizard after he mocks her.

Ascalaphus.note: Ascalaphus is a son of Ares whose death provokes his father’s rage.
Demeter pins Ascalaphus beneath a stone for reporting Persephone’s pomegranate consumption.

Ascanius.note: Cupid assumes Ascanius's appearance while Venus conceals the boy.

Asia.note: Asia replaces Clymene as Atlas's mother in this later genealogy.

Asia.myth: Two personified continents struggle over Europa
Asia.note: Personified Asia claims Europa as her child but loses her to the western land destined by Zeus.
Asia replaces Clymene as mother of Iapetus's four principal sons.
Pseudo-Apollodorus names the Oceanid Asia as Menoetius’s mother.
Apollodorus gives Asia as Oceanus's daughter and Iapetus's consort.
Asia replaces Clymene as Prometheus's mother by Iapetus.
Herodotus instead places Asia as Prometheus's wife.

Asklepios.note: Athena gives Asklepios Medusa’s opposed healing and killing blood after her death.
Asklepios restores Ploutos’ sight during temple incubation using sacred snakes.

Asopis.note: Later traditions name Asopis as a partner of Iapetus.

Asteres.note: The stars follow the plunging solar orb while Hemera is displaced.

Asterion.note: Asterion attends Astraeus and brings his revolving celestial sphere.
The Cretan king marries Europa and raises her sons.

Astraea.note: One disputed genealogy makes the constellation Maiden Astraeus’s daughter.

Astynome.note: Astynome is one of the competing mothers assigned to Cycnus by Ares.

Astyochus.note: Astyochus is one of Aeolus' six colonizing sons.

Atalanta.note: Venus transforms Atalanta into a lion after being denied thanks.

Atargatis.note: Hellenistic and Roman interpretation locally equated Aphrodite with Atargatis.

Athamas.note: Athamas is listed among the sons of Aeolus and Enarete.

Athena Alea.note: Mnemosyne and the Muses appeared on an altar in Athena Alea’s sanctuary.

Athena Ergane.note: Ploutos stands beside Athena Ergane, associating skilled work with prosperity.

Athena Paionia.note: Their images were displayed together in the same Athenian sanctuary complex.

Atreus.note: Helios reverses course as the divine sign confirming Atreus's kingship.

Attis.note: Attis becomes associated with Rhea only through her identification with Cybele.

Augeas.note: Later catalogues sometimes count Augeas among Helios's children.

Aura.note: Artemis appeals to Nemesis after Aura mocks her body.

Aurae.note: Aurae restrain or guide Selene’s horses in funerary imagery.

Auson.note: Western genealogy variously makes Auson Calypso's child by Odysseus or Atlas.

Auster.note: Roman translation and poetry equate Notus with the southern wind Auster.

Autolycus.note: Later mythography makes Autolycus a son of Hermes and Chione or Philonis.

Autonoë.note: Harmonia is the mother of Autonoë.

Balius.note: Zephyrus fathers the immortal horse Balius by Podarge.
Podarge bears the immortal horse Balius to Zephyrus.
Zephyrus fathers the immortal horse Balius upon Podarge.

Basileia.note: Diodorus’s Atlantic account presents Basileia and Hyperion as siblings.
Basileia marries Hyperion and bears Helios and Selene before her brothers murder him.
The euhemeristic Atlantic narrative makes Basileia mother of Selene and Helios.

Battus.note: Hermes turns Battus to stone after he breaks his promise of silence.

Bellerophon.note: Bellerophon confronts the Chimera as the first supposedly fatal Lycian ordeal.
Bellerophon kills the Chimera by obeying divine portents.
After repeated capture attempts, Bellerophon bridles Pegasus with Athena’s aid.
Pegasus carries Bellerophon during his campaigns against monstrous and martial enemies.
Pegasus throws Bellerophon down when he attempts to reach Zeus’s dwelling.

Bendis.note: Greeks compared Artemis with Bendis, though the Thracian goddess remained separately named.
Hecate is contextually equated with Bendis in cultic or magical interpretation.

Benthesicyme.note: Later mythography makes Benthesicyme a daughter of Amphitrite and Poseidon.
Later mythography names Benthesicyme among Poseidon and Amphitrite’s children.

Bia.note: Ananke and Bia share a sanctuary into which entry was not customary.
Bia is Nike’s sibling, born to Pallas and Styx.

Bia.date: late eighth or early seventh century BCE

Bia.note: Bia silently assists Kratos and Hephaestus during Prometheus's chaining.
Bia is the daughter of Styx and Pallas.
Styx brings Bia to Zeus, beside whom she remains.

Boeotus.note: Aeolus son of Poseidon is the twin brother of Boeotus.

Boutes.note: A local or later tradition names Boutes as Aphrodite's lover.

Branchus.note: Branchus is named among Apollo's male beloveds.

Breath.note: Chronos generates Breath or Wind from his own seed.

Briareos.note: Briareos emerges from Erebus to assist Zeus in the Titanomachy.
Poseidon gives his daughter Cymopoleia to Briareos in marriage.
Briareos awards Poseidon the Isthmus and Helios Acrocorinth.
Summoned by Thetis, Briareos prevents a divine coup against Zeus.

Briareus.note: Virgil places Chimera and Briareus together among infernal apparitions.
Briareus and Crius share Gaia and Uranus as parents.
Crius is collectively implicated when the Titans release Briareus from imprisonment.
Briareus joins Zeus and helps overwhelm Cronos’s Titan faction with stones.
Briareus guards the sleeping, bound Cronos on a western island.
Gaia bears the Hundred-Hander Briareus by Uranus.
Gaia advises Zeus to free Briareus, whose aid secures victory.
Briareus arbitrates Helios's territorial dispute with Poseidon.
Briareus's arrival ends Hera, Athena, and Poseidon's conspiracy against Zeus.
Briareus fights the Titans on Zeus’s side; Hyperion’s individual participation is inferred.
After fighting the Titans, Briareus guards their prison at Tartarus.
Thetis summons the hundred-handed Briareus, whose presence frightens Zeus’s conspirators.
Briareus is a Hundred-Hander son of Uranus and Gaia.
Uranus conceals Briareus within Gaia; later tradition describes binding.

Brimo.note: Brimo is a shared mystery and magical name applied contextually to Hecate.

Britomartis.note: Artemis saves her favorite companion after Britomartis leaps into fishing nets.
Artemis makes Britomartis divine under the title Diktynna.

Bromios.note: Imperial cosmic systematization includes Bromios among identities folded into Pan.

Brontes.note: Young Artemis playfully pulls the Cyclops Brontes’ chest hair.
Brontes and Crius share Gaia and Uranus as parents.
Gaia bears the Cyclops Brontes by Uranus.
A rare scholium makes Brontes, rather than Zeus, Athena's father by Metis.
Brontes is a Cyclops son of Uranus and Gaia.
Uranus conceals Brontes within Gaia; later tradition describes binding.

Buphagus.note: Iapetus fathers Buphagus by Thornax in Arcadian genealogy.

Butes.note: Butes is Boreas's son by an unnamed mother.
Their voices entice Butes to abandon the Argo and swim toward them.

Cabeiri.note: Hephaestus fathers or ancestrally generates the Cabeiri through Cabeiro.

Cabeiro.note: Lemnian and Samothracian genealogy makes Cabeiro Hephaestus's partner.
Pherecydes’ regional genealogy identifies Cabeiro as Proteus’ daughter.

Cadmus.note: Cadmus serves Ares for eight years after killing the god’s sacred dragon.
Cadmus marries Ares’s daughter Harmonia after completing service to Ares.
Under the Agenor genealogy, Cadmus is Europa’s brother.
Agenor sends Cadmus to recover Europa; he instead follows an oracle and founds Thebes.
Harmonia becomes the immortal wife of the mortal Theban founder.
Harmonia and Cadmus are both transformed into serpents.
Harmonia accompanies Cadmus as he aids the Encheleans against Illyrians.
Harmonia embraces Cadmus and asks to share his serpent fate.
Nike serves as bridesmaid and victory-crier at Cadmus’s wedding.
Cadmus promises a victory-song and tricks Typhon into yielding Zeus's sinews.
Cadmus subdues Typhon's attention with deceptive pastoral music.

Caelus.note: Aether and Dies are parents of Caelus.
Latin literary mythology equates Greek Uranus with the Roman personified Sky.

Caenis.note: Poseidon has intercourse with Caenis before granting her transformative wish.
Poseidon transforms Caenis into the invulnerable man Caeneus at her request.

Caicus.note: Caicus is a river son of Tethys and Oceanus.

Calais.note: Boreas and Oreithyia are parents of the winged Boread Calais.
Calais is a winged son of Boreas and Oreithyia.
Calais chases and repels the Harpies after their attack on Phineus's meal.
One early tradition reports that Zetes and Calais kill the Harpies.
Iris stops Calais from killing the Harpies and swears they will withdraw.

Calchus.note: Circe drugs her unwanted suitor into madness and confines him in a pigsty.
Circe releases Calchus after he swears never to return to Aeaea.

Caligo.note: Caligo and Chaos produce Aether, Night, Day, and Erebus.
Caligo produces Chaos in the late Roman mythographic genealogy.
Chaos reproduces with Caligo, generating Night, Day, Erebus, and Aether.
Roman mythography makes Nox a child of Chaos and Caligo.
Roman genealogy makes Mors the child of Nox and Caligo.

Calliope.note: Calliope is a daughter of Mnemosyne and Zeus.
In a variant, Calliope adjudicates Persephone’s dispute with Aphrodite over Adonis.
Later commentary traditions sometimes name Calliope as their mother.
Calliope and Urania are daughters of Zeus and Mnemosyne.

Calliope.myth: Cicadas report philosophers to the Muses
Calliope.note: Calliope and Urania jointly receive reports concerning philosophical mortals.

Callirhoe.note: Possible mother if Callirhoe is the antecedent of Hesiod’s feminine pronoun.

Callirhoe.myth: Callirhoe pleads that Geryon avoid Heracles
Callirhoe.note: She exposes her nursing breast and begs Geryon not to fight.
Callirhoe is an Oceanid daughter of Tethys and Oceanus.

Callisto.note: Artemis shoots Callisto after Hera changes her into a bear.
One variant makes Artemis transform Callisto for failing to preserve virginity.
Diana expels the pregnant Callisto from her company.
Tethys refuses to receive transformed Callisto into Ocean because Callisto offended Hera.

Callithyia.note: Tzetzes names Callithyia among Aeolus' twelve intermarried children.

Calyce.note: Calyce is listed among the daughters of Aeolus and Enarete.

Camenae.note: Roman literature and religion equate the indigenous Camenae with the Greek Muses.

Campe.note: Campe guards the imprisoned Cyclopes until Zeus kills her.
Campe guards the Hundred-Handers while they remain imprisoned in Tartarus.
Cronus appoints Campe to guard Tartarus until Zeus kills her.

Canace.note: Canace is listed as a daughter of Aeolus.
Aeolus sends Canace a sword, effectively commanding her suicide.
Tzetzes includes Canace among the named children of Homeric Aeolus.

Cancer.note: The giant crab fights beside the Hydra and bites Heracles's foot.

Candalus.note: Candalus is listed among Helios's Rhodian sons.

Capaneus.note: Asclepius raises Capaneus from the dead in an early variant.

Capheira.note: Rhea entrusts infant Poseidon to Capheira and the Telchines.

Carnabon.note: Demeter punishes Carnabon for attacking Triptolemus.

Carnus.note: Marginal genealogical sources occasionally make Carnus Europa’s son by Zeus.

Carpus.note: Later accounts make Carpus the child of Zephyrus and Chloris.
Later mythographic tradition makes personified Fruit the son of Zephyrus and Chloris.

Carystus.note: Late genealogical sources occasionally call Carystus a son of Chiron.

Cassandra.note: Apollo grants Cassandra prophecy while expecting a sexual relationship.
Cassandra accepts prophecy but refuses or deceives Apollo concerning sex.
Apollo ensures Cassandra's true prophecies will never be believed.
Some identified Pasiphae with Cassandra, renamed for revealing oracles to all.

Cassiphone.note: Late scholia name Cassiphone as Circe’s daughter, with uncertain paternity.

Catreus.note: Some genealogies list Catreus as Ariadne’s brother.

Caucasian Eagle.note: Later enlarged Typhon-Echidna family trees make the eagle her sibling.
Later mythographers inconsistently add the Caucasian Eagle to the Hydra's brood.

Caucasian eagle.note: Late variants assign the Caucasian eagle to Echidna’s brood.
Zeus's winged agent repeatedly consumes Prometheus's liver until Heracles kills it.
Variable later genealogies assign the Caucasian eagle to Typhon.

Celaeno.note: Celaeno is one variant mother of Apollo's son Delphus.
Celaeno is one of Atlas and Pleione's seven daughters.
Celaeno bears Prometheus the sons Lycus and Chimaereus.

Celtus.note: Appian names Celtus as a son of Polyphemus and Galatea.

Centaurs.note: Virgil places Chimera and the Centaurs together among infernal apparitions.

Centaurus.note: Roman astronomical tradition identifies the constellation Centaurus with the catasterized Chiron.

Cephalus.note: Eos unites with Cephalus and bears Phaethon.
Eos pursues and abducts the young hunter despite his marriage to Procris.
Aurora releases Cephalus after making him suspicious of Procris, prompting his disguised fidelity test.
Hemera falls in love with beautiful Cephalus, carries him away, and bears Phaethon.

Ceramus.note: Athenian genealogy makes Ariadne Ceramus’ mother by Dionysus.
Ceramus is attributed to Dionysus and Ariadne.

Cercaphus.note: Cercaphus is listed among Helios's Rhodian sons.

Ceryneian hind.note: Heracles pursues and captures Artemis’s sacred golden-horned deer alive.

Ceto.note: Probably Echidna’s mother, though Hesiod’s grammar leaves the parentage uncertain.
Gaia bears Ceto through union with Pontus.
Ceto and Phorcys beget the Graeae.
Ceto bears the unnamed golden-apple guardian after union with Phorcys.
Ceto and Nereus are children of Pontus and Gaia.
One variant makes Ceto and Phorcys parents of the Hesperides.

Ceyx.note: Aeolus calms the winds while Ceyx and Alcyone nest as birds.

Chariclo.note: Chariclo is Chiron's wife and companion in Hellenistic and Roman tradition.

Charis.note: Charis is Hephaestus's wife and receives Thetis in their palace.

Chimaereus.note: Late sources make Chimaereus a son of Prometheus and Celaeno.

Chimarrhus.note: Plutarch rationalizes the Chimera as a pirate with animal emblems on his ship.

Chione.note: Boreas and Oreithyia are named as Chione’s parents.
Chione is one variant mother of Apollo's son Philammon.
Chione is a daughter of Boreas and Oreithyia.
Later genealogy names Chione or Philonis as Hermes's lover and Autolycus's mother.
A late tradition makes the nymph Chione Priapus's mother by Dionysus.

Chrysaor.note: Possible father if Hesiod’s feminine subject is interpreted as Callirhoe.
Chrysaor springs from Medusa alongside Pegasus at her death.
Pegasus and Chrysaor are co-born from the beheaded Medusa.
Chrysaor springs from Medusa after Poseidon fathered him.

Chthon/Earth.note: Euripides calls the winged Sirens virgin daughters of Earth.

Chthoniē.note: Chthoniē and Chronos coexist eternally; no sexual union is stated.

Cilix.note: Under the Agenor genealogy, Cilix is Europa’s brother.
Cilix fails to recover Europa and becomes the eponym of Cilicia.

Cithaeronian lion.note: A rival tradition derives Heracles’ lion skin from a Cithaeronian beast.

Cleito.note: Poseidon mates with Cleito and encloses her hill with concentric rings.

Cleitus.note: Eos carries off beautiful Cleitus so that he may dwell among immortals.

Cleopatra.note: Boreas and Oreithyia are named as Cleopatra’s parents.
Cleopatra is a daughter of Boreas and Oreithyia.

Clio.note: Clio is a daughter of Mnemosyne and Zeus.
Clio and Urania are daughters of Zeus and Mnemosyne.

Clymene.note: Tzetzes names Clymene among Aeolus' twelve intermarried children.
Clymene is Atlas's mother in Hesiod's genealogy.
Clymene bears Epimetheus and his three brothers.
Clymene bears Helios's son Phaethon while married to Merops.
Clymene joins Iapetus and bears his four principal sons.
Hesiod names the Oceanid Clymene as Menoetius’s mother.
Hesiod makes Clymene Oceanus's daughter and Iapetus's consort.
Clymene is Prometheus's mother by Iapetus.
A late genealogy makes Prometheus the child of Uranus and Clymene.
Clymene is an Oceanid daughter of Tethys and Oceanus.

Clymenus.note: Tzetzes names Clymenus among Aeolus' twelve intermarried children.

Clytemnestra.note: Later genealogies count Clytemnestra among the twins' sisters.

Clytie.note: Helios rejects Clytie, who wastes away turning toward him.

Clytius.note: Hecate kills the Giant Clytius with torches or firebrands.
Clytius shoots down one member of the projectile-feathered flock.

Cocytus.note: The same mountain water is said to feed both Styx and Cocytus.

Colchian dragon.note: A dragon belonging to Ares guards his sacred Colchian field.
Hyginus assigns the Colchian dragon to Typhon and Echidna.

Conisalus.note: Strabo describes the Attic ithyphallic Conisalus as resembling Priapus.

Constantinople.note: Constantinople’s personification developed as a Tyche-like civic figure.

Coronis.note: Coronis becomes pregnant with Apollo's son Asclepius.
Some versions make Apollo, rather than Artemis, kill the pregnant Coronis.
Coronis bears Asclepius before dying during his birth tradition.

Cottus.note: Cottus and Crius share Gaia and Uranus as parents.
Crius is collectively implicated when the Titans release Cottus from imprisonment.
Cottus joins Zeus and helps overwhelm Cronos’s Titan faction with stones.
Cottus emerges from Erebus to assist Zeus in the Titanomachy.
Gaia bears the Hundred-Hander Cottus by Uranus.
Gaia advises Zeus to free Cottus, whose aid secures victory.
Cottus fights the Titans on Zeus’s side; Hyperion’s individual participation is inferred.
After fighting the Titans, Cottus guards their prison at Tartarus.
Cottus is a Hundred-Hander son of Uranus and Gaia.
Uranus conceals Cottus within Gaia; later tradition describes binding.

Courage.note: Courage accompanies Penia’s antagonistic entourage and intimidates Ploutos.

Crataeis.note: Scylla is her daughter; Circe advises invoking her against another attack.

Cres.note: Cinaethon's genealogy makes Hephaestus the grandson of Cres through Talos.
A genealogical Talos, possibly distinct from the guardian, is named as Cres’s son.

Cretan Bull.note: The supernatural bull sent from the sea is the Minotaur's biological father.

Cretan bull.note: Heracles captures the bull alive before it is released.

Crete.note: Late compilations sometimes assign Europa an eponymous daughter named Crete.

Cretheus.note: Cretheus is listed among the sons of Aeolus and Enarete.

Creusa.note: Apollo sexually encounters Creusa; she condemns his conduct after abandoning their child.
As Mother of the Gods, Rhea and Aphrodite save Creusa from enslavement.

Crommyonian Sow.note: An uncertain systematization makes the boar her offspring; this genealogy was never stable.
Later enlarged Typhon-Echidna family trees make the sow her sibling.
Later mythographers inconsistently add the Crommyonian Sow to the Hydra's brood.

Cronus.note: Cronus fathers Chiron on Philyra, assuming equine form in later accounts.
Cronus and Crius share Gaia and Uranus as parents.
Crius and the victorious Titans collectively give sovereignty to Cronus.
Cronus releases the Cyclopes during his revolt against Uranus.
After gaining power, Cronus confines the Cyclopes again.
Olen's lost hymn reportedly described Eileithyia as older than Cronus.
His attack on Uranus indirectly causes their generation from spilled blood.
Gaia bears Cronus by Uranus.
Gaia arms and conceals Cronus so he can castrate Uranus.
Gaia and Uranus foretell that Zeus will overthrow Cronus.
Cronus’s castration of Uranus causes the Gigantes’ generation.
Hopladamos’s Arcadian Giants defend Rhea from Cronus.
Glaucus gains immortality from dog’s-tooth grass originally sown by Cronus.
Cronus is Hades’ father in the dominant early genealogy.
Cronus swallows Hades after birth before Zeus forces their release.
Cronus is their Titan brother in the Gaia–Uranus genealogy.
They fight and defeat the Titan faction led by Cronus.
Hera is the daughter of Cronus in the dominant genealogy.
Cronus swallows Hera together with his other children.
Cronus is Hestia's father.
Cronus swallows Hestia after her birth to prevent his overthrow.
Tzetzes records Cronus and Night as parents of the Fates.
Metis allegedly supplies or helps administer the drug that makes Cronus disgorge his children.
Momus writes provocative praise of Cronus, implicitly attacking Zeus's order.
Rhapsodic Nyx nurtures Cronus during the divine succession.
A Byzantine variant pairs Nyx with Cronus as parents of the Moirai.
Cronus and Oceanus are Titan sons of Gaia and Uranus.
Cronus and Phoebe are children of Gaia and Uranus.
Cronus fathers, swallows, and later disgorges Poseidon.
Cronus is invoked as an underworld witness alongside Styx in Hera’s oath.
Cronus is confined in Tartarus with the defeated Titans.
Tethys and Cronus are sibling Titans.
Cronus and Theia are children of Gaia and Uranus.

Crotus.note: Some later genealogies make Crotus the son of Pan and Eupheme.

Curete.note: Diodorus preserves a Cretan alternative making Hyperion the son of a Curete.

Curetes.note: Rhea entrusts Zeus to the Curetes, who conceal his cries with shields.

Cyane.note: The Liparian Aeolus marries Cyane, daughter of Liparus.

Cycnus.note: Cycnus is Ares’s violent son in the Heracles cycle.
Ares intervenes in battle after Heracles kills his son Cycnus.
Heracles kills Ares’ son Cycnus in battle.

Cyllene.note: Cyllene defends the prodigious infant and explains his newly invented lyre.

Cymatolege.note: Amphitrite and Cymatolege jointly calm waves and hush violent winds.

Cymodoce.note: Amphitrite and Cymodoce jointly calm waves and hush violent winds.

Cymopoleia.note: Poseidon's daughter Cymopoleia becomes the wife of Briareus.
Poseidon gives Cymopoleia in marriage to Briareos.

Cyparissus.note: Cyparissus is named among Apollo's male beloveds.

Cyrene.note: Apollo takes Cyrene to Libya, where she bears Aristaeus.
One genealogy makes Cyrene the mother by Ares of Diomedes of Thrace.
Cyrene reveals Proteus’ sleeping place and teaches Aristaeus how to bind him.

Daedalus.note: Daedalus constructs Ariadne’s celebrated dancing place at Knossos.
Daedalus advises Ariadne to give Theseus the thread for escape.

Danubian Rider Gods.note: Provincial rider gods borrow Dioscuric iconography, although their identity remains debated.

Daphne.note: Driven by Cupid's arrow, Apollo pursues Daphne until she becomes laurel.
Eros strikes Daphne with a lead-tipped arrow that produces aversion to love.
One account identifies Pasiphae with Daphne, the prophetic daughter of Amyclas.

Dardanus.note: Atlas is Dardanus's ancestor through his daughter Electra.

Death.note: Apollo confronts Death verbally over the impending death of Alcestis.

Deino.note: Later mythography names Deino as a third Graia among Medusa’s close kin.

Deion.note: Deion is listed among the sons of Aeolus and Enarete.

Deiopea.note: Juno promises Deiopea to Aeolus as wife, but no marriage follows.

Deiphobe.note: Virgil calls Deiphobe daughter of Glaucus, probably the sea-god.

Delos.note: Asteria's transformed, continuing divine body is identified as the island Delos.
Personified Delos accepts Leto and provides a birthplace for Apollo.
Leto promises Delos Apollo's temple and prosperity for receiving her.

Delphic dragoness.note: The Delphic dragoness receives and rears Hera's newborn Typhaon.

Delphinus.note: Delphinus finds Amphitrite, persuades her to marry Poseidon, and conducts the wedding.

Delphus.note: Apollo fathers Delphus in localized genealogies with several variant mothers.

Delphyne.note: Hermes steals Zeus's sinews from the Corycian cave guarded by Delphyne.
Later tradition and scholarship identify Python's Delphic victim-form with the similarly named Cilician dragoness.

Delphyne.myth: Zeus imprisoned in the Corycian cave
Delphyne.note: Delphyne guards Zeus's severed sinews for Typhon.

Demarous.note: Pontus defeats and drives off the attacking Demarous.
Demarous.date: Roman Empire; preserved early fourth century

Demogorgon.note: Boccaccio places Clotho within a learned genealogy descending from Demogorgon.

Demonice.note: Demonice bears Evenus, Molus, Pylus, and Thestius to Ares.

Demophon.note: Demeter treats Demophon with ambrosia and fire, attempting to make him ageless.

Despoina.note: The Phigalian and Lycosuran tradition makes Despoina Demeter’s daughter by Poseidon.
Poseidon fathers Demeter’s mystery-goddess daughter, whose true name remained secret.

Deucalion.note: Deucalion is commonly listed as Ariadne’s brother.
Iapetus is Deucalion's grandfather through Prometheus.
Deucalion is the divine or heroic son of Prometheus.
Prometheus warns Deucalion of Zeus's flood and instructs him to build a provisioned chest.
Zeus sends a flood against Deucalion’s human generation, though Deucalion survives.

Dido.note: Iris cuts Dido’s lock of hair and releases her lingering spirit.

Dike.note: Clarian oracles prescribe joint images of Ares, Dike or Thesmos, and Hermes.

Dike.myth: Dike observes while Ate punishes insolence
Dike.note: Dike sits above while Ate punishes shameless speech, without a narrated meeting.
Dike and Atropos share Zeus and Themis as parents.
Learned traditions conceptually join Dike and the Erinyes as agents of justice.
Dike and Lachesis share Zeus and Themis as parents.

Diomedes.note: Diomedes wounds Ares with a spear, enabled and guided by Athena.
Athena assists Diomedes against Ares and Aphrodite during battle.

Diomedes of Thrace.note: One genealogy makes Diomedes of Thrace the son of Ares and Cyrene.

Dione.note: Dione and Amphitrite attend Leto’s labor together.
Homer identifies Dione as Aphrodite's mother.
Dione receives, comforts, and heals her wounded daughter.
Sporadic genealogical traditions count Dione among Atlas's daughters.
Philo’s Phoenician-Greek system presents Dione as Cronos’s sister.
Cronos takes Dione as his wife in Philo’s Phoenician history.
Dione is Dionysus’s mother in a marginal genealogy.
Dione attends Leto's labor before Eileithyia arrives to release the birth.
Pseudo-Apollodorus includes Dione with Hyperion in his Titan sibling catalogue.
Pseudo-Apollodorus adds Dione to Phoebe's generation of Titanides.
Phoibiē and Dione occupy two angles of the triple magical figure.
Dione is an Oceanid daughter of Tethys and Oceanus.
Pseudo-Apollodorus includes Dione among the Titan daughters with Theia.
Dione is Zeus’s consort at Dodona and Aphrodite’s mother in Homer.

Dolops.note: Hyginus exceptionally lists Dolops as another son of Saturn and Philyra.

Dolphins.note: A late hymn poetically calls dolphins Amphitrite’s offspring or nurslings.

Dolus.note: Roman catalogues make Dolus a child of Erebus and Night.

Doris.note: Hesiod names Amphitrite among the daughters of Doris and Nereus.
A late hymn identifies Amphitrite with Doris and makes her mother of the Nereids.
Asteria as Delos is said to have been consecrated first to Doris.
A possibly homonymous Calypso is catalogued among Nereus and Doris's Nereids.
Hesiod makes Doris the mother of the fifty Nereids.
Nereus and the Oceanid Doris generate the fifty Nereids.
Pergamene sculpture places Nereus and Doris among the divine combatants.
Doris and Nereus are parents of the fifty Nereids.
Doris is an Oceanid daughter of Oceanus and Tethys.
Doris is an Oceanid daughter of Tethys and Oceanus.
Doris, an Oceanid daughter of Oceanus, is Thetis’s mother.

Dorus.note: Dorus and Aeolus are sons of Hellen and Orseis.

Draco.note: Astraeus interprets Draco as a celestial factor in Persephone’s horoscope.
Astronomical mythography identifies the Hesperidean guardian with the constellation Draco.

Dryas.note: Dryas is named among Ares’s children in varying genealogical traditions.
Dryas is named as an additional son of Iapetus.

Dysnomia.note: Eris bears Dysnomia without a named father.

Earth.note: Earth or congealed matter generates the primordial serpent Chronos with Water.

Ecbasus.note: Pseudo-Apollodorus places Argus after Ecbasus in the Argive royal succession.

Echo.note: Pan maddens shepherds who tear apart Echo after she rejects him.
Echo appears amicably with Pan as his musical and erotic companion.

Eidothea.note: Homer identifies Eidothea as Proteus’ daughter.
Eidothea teaches Menelaus the ambush and supplies disguising sealskins and ambrosia.

Eioneus.note: Late and textually fragile genealogies identify Eioneus as Proteus’ son.

Eirene.note: Eirene and Atropos share Zeus and Themis as parents.
Images of Hestia and Eirene stood together in Athens's prytaneion.
Eirene and Lachesis share Zeus and Themis as parents.
Eirene cradles and nurtures Ploutos, representing prosperity produced by peace.

Electra.note: Electra is one of Atlas and Pleione's seven daughters.
The Samothracian account makes Electra Harmonia's mother.
Electra raises Harmonia as her foster daughter on Samothrace.
Electra bears Iris, Aello and Ocypete to Thaumas.
The Oceanid Electra is Iris’s mother in the Hesiodic genealogy.
Electra.date: late eighth or seventh century BCE

Electra.note: Electra is an Oceanid daughter of Oceanus and Tethys.
Electra is an Oceanid daughter of Tethys and Oceanus.
Electra and Tyche belong to the company of Oceanid sisters.
Electra and Tyche gather flowers and play among Persephone’s Oceanid companions.
Electra is listed among Zeus’s important partners.

Electryone.note: Later Rhodian accounts make Electryone a daughter of Helios and Rhodos.

Eleos.note: Hyginus’s expanded genealogy makes Eleos a child of Erebus and Night.

Elpenor.note: Circe helps Odysseus’s company perform burial rites for Elpenor on Aeaea.

Emathion.note: Later epic and mythography name Emathion as Eos's son by Tithonus.

Enarete.note: Enarete is the wife of Aeolus son of Hellen.

Enceladus.note: Athena crushes the giant Enceladus beneath Sicily.

Endeis.note: Scholia sometimes make Endeis Chiron and Chariclo's daughter, contrary to other genealogies.

Endymion.note: Hypnos loves Endymion and keeps his eyes open during sleep.
A fragment probably provides the earliest surviving trace of their romance.
Selene burns for Endymion and repeatedly visits his cave at Latmos.
The Eleans said Selene loved Endymion and bore him fifty daughters.
Selene stops her chariot, descends, and gazes upon or kisses Endymion.

Enodia.note: The Thessalian road and cemetery goddess Enodia was assimilated to Hecate.

Enyalios.note: Enyalios is sometimes Ares’s epithet or equivalent, but elsewhere an independent god.
Later genealogy sometimes makes Enyalios the child of Ares and Enyo.

Enyalios.myth: Witnesses of the Athenian ephebic oath
Enyalios.note: Enyo and Enyalios are separately named divine witnesses of the military oath.
Late commentary makes Enyalios the son of Enyo and Ares.

Eosphorus.note: Eosphorus is a son of Astraeus and Eos.
Eosphorus sees Demeter approaching and announces her arrival.
Eosphorus and Boreas are children of Eos and Astraeus.
The personified Morning Star is born to Eos and Astraeus.
Notus and Eosphorus share Eos and Astraeus as parents.
Eosphorus follows the winds among the children of Eos and Astraeus.

Epaphus.note: Hyginus’s expanded genealogy makes Epaphus a child of Erebus and Night.

Ephialtes.note: Ephialtes and Otus bind Ares inside a bronze jar for thirteen months.
As a deer, Artemis runs between the brothers, causing mutual slaughter.
Ephialtes institutes sacrifice to Melete, Mneme, and Aoide on Helicon.
Poseidon fathers the giant Ephialtes with Iphimedeia.

Ephyra.note: A Corinthian genealogical variant makes Ephyra the wife of Epimetheus.

Epione.note: Epione is Asclepius' wife and cult companion.

Epiphron.note: Hyginus’s expanded genealogy makes Epiphron a child of Erebus and Night.

Erato.note: Erato is a daughter of Mnemosyne and Zeus.
Erato and Urania are daughters of Zeus and Mnemosyne.

Erechtheus.note: Athenian cult closely fuses Poseidon with the ancestral figure Erechtheus.

Eriboea.note: Eriboea alerts Hermes, enabling the imprisoned Ares’s rescue.

Erichthonius.note: Athena guards Gaia’s child Erichthonius and hides him in a chest.
Boreas assumes stallion form and sires twelve supernatural fillies from Erichthonius's mares.
Gaia conceives and bears the autochthonous Erichthonius.
Gaia presents the newborn Erichthonius to Athena.
Hephaestus fathers Erichthonius when his semen impregnates Earth.

Eridanus.note: Eridanus is named among Oceanus's river sons.
Eridanus is a river son of Tethys and Oceanus.

Erikepaios.note: Orphic systematization assimilates Dionysus to Erikepaios.
Imperial cosmic systematization includes Erikepaios among identities folded into Pan.

Eros.note: Eros and Aether share Erebus and Nyx as parents.
An unnamed goddess creates Eros; identifying her as Ananke is disputed.
Alcaeus’ poetic genealogy makes Eros the child of Zephyrus and Iris.
Winged Eros mingles reproductively with Chaos, producing the race of birds.
A statue of Eros shares the Charites’ cult pedestal at Elis.
The Gratiae diffuse balsam during Eros and Psyche’s wedding.
Eros accompanies or motivates Dionysus’s erotic adventures.
Olen's lost Delian hymn reportedly made Eileithyia the mother of Eros.
Eros flies above the probable Epimetheus and Pandora reception scene.
Eros emerges from the cosmic egg deposited in Erebus’s bosom.
Acusilaus reportedly makes Eros a child of Erebus and Nyx.
Roman catalogues make Eros a child of Erebus and Night.

Eros.myth: Eros directs Zeus’s desire for Europa
Eros.note: Eros wounds or directs Zeus with desire and accompanies Europa’s sea-crossing.
Eros handles bridal adornment near Harmonia and Aphrodite.
Eros acts as an active force bringing about Harmonia's marriage.
Eros attends the marriage of Heracles and Hebe in some representations.
Eros is Iris’s son by Zephyrus in an isolated archaic genealogy.
Metis is Eros's grandmother through her son Poros.
One Acusilean testimony makes Night and Aether parents of Eros.
Nyx lays a wind-egg in Erebus from which Eros hatches.
Eros intervenes during Pan’s resisted approach to Aphrodite.
Imperial cosmic systematization includes Eros among identities folded into Pan.
Later Orphic exposition explicitly equates primordial Eros with Phanes.
Lucian presents Eros as Priapus's maternal brother through Aphrodite.
Later psychoanalysis opposes a death drive called Thanatos to Eros.
Winged Eros stands beside Tyche, signifying Fortune’s supremacy in love.

Eros.myth: Hymenaeus competes with Eros at kottabos
Eros.note: Urania's handmade globe is offered during Hymenaeus' game against Eros.
A fragmentary poetic variant names Eros as Zephyrus’ child by Iris.

Erotes.note: Nike dances beside the Erotes during the wedding celebration.
Erotes accompany Selene during her descent toward Endymion.

Error.note: Juno proposes summoning Discordia together with Error from the underworld.

Ersa.note: A fragmentary genealogy makes Zeus and Selene parents of Ersa.

Erysichthon.note: Demeter condemns Erysichthon to insatiable hunger after he cuts her sacred grove.

Erytheia.note: A later Sardinian genealogy makes Erytheia Geryon's daughter.

Eryx.note: A later variant makes Eryx the son of Aphrodite and Poseidon.

Euanthes.note: Some mythographic genealogies attribute Euanthes to Ariadne.

Euboea.note: Euboea, daughter of Larymnus, is named Glaucus' mother.

Eubouleus.note: Eubouleus shares Eleusinian ritual space and representations with Plouton and Kore.
Orphic Hymn 29 ambiguously makes Persephone mother of many-formed Eubouleus.
Eubouleus receives purified initiates beside Persephone in the Thurii funerary tablets.
A disputed interpretation of the late Orphic hymn derives Tyche from Eubouleus.

Eucharis.note: Calypso becomes jealous when Telemachus forms an attachment to the nymph Eucharis.

Euchenor.note: Tzetzes names Euchenor among Aeolus' twelve intermarried children.

Eucleia.note: Late Neoplatonic tradition makes Aglaea and Hephaestus parents of Eucleia.
Late Neoplatonic genealogy makes Eucleia a daughter of Hephaestus and Aglaea.

Euenus.note: Euenus is a river son of Tethys and Oceanus.

Eukles.note: Eukles receives purified initiates beside Persephone in the Thurii funerary tablets.

Eumolpus.note: Inscribed vase scenes place Eumolpus and Amphitrite in the same divine assembly or banquet.
Boreas is Eumolpus’ grandfather through Chione and Poseidon.

Eunomia.note: An individual late or local genealogy assigns Eunomia to Aphrodite.
Eunomia and Atropos share Zeus and Themis as parents.
Eunomia replaces Eurynome as mother of the triad.
Eunomia and Lachesis share Zeus and Themis as parents.

Eupheme.note: Late Neoplatonic tradition makes Aglaea and Hephaestus parents of Eupheme.
Late Neoplatonic genealogy makes Eupheme a daughter of Hephaestus and Aglaea.
Eupheme is sometimes paired with Pan as Crotus’s mother.

Euphemus.note: Disguised as Eurypylus, Triton gives Euphemus earth securing his descendants’ Libyan claim.

Euphrosyne.note: Hyginus’s expanded genealogy makes Euphrosyne a child of Erebus and Night.
Hyginus adds Euphrosyne to Nox's expanded offspring catalogue.

Euryale.note: Euryale is a Gorgon sister of the Graeae.
Euryale is Medusa’s immortal Gorgon sister.
Euryale laments Medusa while the Gorgons’ serpents hiss.
Euryale pursues Perseus after he beheads Medusa.

Eurybia.note: Eurybia is Astraeus’s mother in the Hesiodic genealogy.
Their sexual union produces Astraeus, Pallas, and Perses.
Gaia bears Eurybia through union with Pontus.
Eurybia and Nereus are children of Pontus and Gaia.

Eurybia.date: late eighth or early seventh century BCE

Eurybia.note: Pontus fathers iron-hearted Eurybia with Gaia.

Eurydice.note: Hades conditionally releases Eurydice, but she returns when Orpheus looks back.

Eurygone.note: Tzetzes names Eurygone among Aeolus' twelve intermarried children.

Eurymedon.note: Eurymedon rules the reckless race of Gigantes as their king.
A late learned genealogy makes the Titan Eurymedon his father.

Eurynome.note: Eurynome bears the canonical triad to Zeus.
Cronos and Rhea displace Eurynome from rule and cast her into Ocean.
Eurynome joins Thetis in concealing and fostering Hephaestus beneath Ocean.
Hesiod names Eurynome among Oceanus's Oceanid daughters.
Rhea helps depose Eurynome from cosmic rule.
Rhea wrestles Eurynome and casts her into Tartarus.
Eurynome is an Oceanid daughter of Tethys and Oceanus.
Thetis and Eurynome jointly conceal and foster the rejected Hephaestus.
Eurynome bears the Charites to Zeus.

Euryphaessa.note: Euryphaessa is Selene’s mother in an alternate hymnic genealogy.

Eurystheus.myth: Manipulated births of Heracles and Eurystheus
Eurystheus.note: Eileithyia's birth power enables Eurystheus' premature delivery and precedence over Heracles.

Eurytion.note: Eurytion tends Geryon's herd and dies defending it from Heracles.
Orthrus and Eurytion jointly guard the herd; Eurytion comes to his aid.

Euterpe.note: Euterpe is a daughter of Mnemosyne and Zeus.
Euterpe and Urania are daughters of Zeus and Mnemosyne.

Euthenia.note: Late Neoplatonic tradition makes Aglaea and Hephaestus parents of Euthenia.
Late Neoplatonic genealogy makes Euthenia a daughter of Hephaestus and Aglaea.

Evenus.note: Evenus is a son of Ares and Demonice in Apollodoran genealogy.

Fate.note: Fate assigns Proteus custody of the sea’s keys.

Fates.note: Apollo tricks the Fates into permitting a substitute death for Admetus.

Fatum.note: Roman catalogues make Fate a child of Erebus and Night.

Favonius.note: Roman poetry regularly equates the Latin west-wind god Favonius with Zephyrus.

Fire.note: Chronos generates Fire from his own seed.

Fontes.note: Hyginus lists the personified Springs among Pallas and Styx’s offspring.
Hyginus’s corrupt expanded genealogy lists Fontes among Styx’s offspring.

Fraus.note: Roman catalogues make Fraud a child of Erebus and Night.

Friendship.note: Hyginus lists Friendship among Nox's expanded offspring.

Furor.note: Juno proposes summoning Discordia together with Furor from the underworld.

Galas.note: Appian names Galas as a son of Polyphemus and Galatea.

Galatea.note: Polyphemus courts Galatea through pastoral song, but his desire remains frustrated.
Galatea provocatively teases Polyphemus while he pretends indifference.
Polyphemus courts and violently pursues Galatea, who loves Acis instead.
Galatea is one of the Nereids fathered by Nereus.
Polyphemus courts Galatea through music, but their relationship remains uncertain.

Galatea.myth: The lovesick shepherd sings to Galatea
Galatea.note: He offers Galatea pastoral gifts and cave life but remains unsuccessful.

Galatea.myth: Galatea teasingly pursues an indifferent Polyphemus
Galatea.note: Galatea throws apples and provokes him while he feigns indifference.

Galatea.myth: Polyphemus and Galatea appear as affectionate lovers
Galatea.note: Campanian paintings depict mutual affection, correspondence, or erotic union.
Appian makes Galatea Polyphemus’s mate and mother of their sons.

Galatea.myth: Polyphemus establishes Galatea’s shrine near Etna
Galatea.note: Duris reportedly credited him with founding her shrine amid pastoral abundance.

Galene.note: Galene is one of the Nereids fathered by Nereus.

Galinthias.note: Galinthias falsely announces delivery, tricking Eileithyia into relaxing her obstructive posture.
Eileithyia punishes the deceiver by transforming her into a weasel or polecat.

Ge.note: Ge and Ploutos are invoked together in the women’s festival prayer.

Genetyllis.note: Later learned tradition partially equates the generative childbirth power Genetyllis with Eileithyia.

Geras.note: Geras and Atropos are siblings under Hesiod's Night genealogy.
Heracles clubs or wrestles the personification of Old Age.
Geras and the Keres are related Night-born banes.

Geras.myth: Two Keres of old age and death
Geras.note: A Kēr bringing old age stands beside another Kēr bringing death.
Hesiod makes Geras and Momus fatherless children of Nyx.
Geras and Nemesis are fatherless children of Nyx.
Nyx bears Geras without a partner.
Geras and Thanatos belong to Nyx's fatherless brood.

Giant.note: Oceanus attacks an unnamed Giant on the Pergamon Altar frieze.

Giants.note: They arise indirectly when blood from Cronos’s assault falls upon Gaia.
Gaia bears both collectives from Uranus’ blood.
Gaia generates the Giants from Uranus’s blood.
Gaia seeks an herb to protect her Giant sons from destruction.
A disputed Pergamon figure conventionally called Nyx attacks a Giant.
Rhea recruits Hopladamus's Giants as protection against Cronus.
A fragmentarily identified Tethys probably fights the Giants beside Oceanus.
The Giants arise when Uranus's blood falls upon Gaia.

Glycon.note: Alexander presents Glycon as a manifestation or new Asclepius.

Golden Dog.note: Rhea appoints the golden dog to guard Amalthea.

Golden female attendants.note: Hephaestus fashions animated golden attendants possessing speech, knowledge, strength, and motion.

Gorgon.note: Deimos and Phobos surround the Gorgon’s glaring face on the shield.

Gorgons.note: Virgil places Chimera and the Gorgons together among infernal apparitions.

Granicus.note: Granicus is a river son of Tethys and Oceanus.

Grannus.note: Roman provincial dedications pair Apollo with the Celtic healing god Grannus.

Gratia.note: Roman catalogues make Favor a child of Erebus and Night.

Gyes.note: Gyes and Crius share Gaia and Uranus as parents.
Crius is collectively implicated when the Titans release Gyes from imprisonment.
After fighting the Titans, Gyes guards their prison at Tartarus.
Gyes is a Hundred-Hander son of Uranus and Gaia.
Uranus conceals Gyes within Gaia; later tradition describes binding.

Gyges.note: Gyges joins Zeus and helps overwhelm Cronos’s Titan faction with stones.
Gyges emerges from Erebus to assist Zeus in the Titanomachy.
Gaia bears the Hundred-Hander Gyges by Uranus.
Gaia advises Zeus to free Gyges, whose aid secures victory.
Gyges fights the Titans on Zeus’s side; Hyperion’s individual participation is inferred.

Hagno.note: The nymph Hagno receives and helps rear infant Poseidon.

Halia.note: A Rhodian tradition makes Poseidon’s relationship with Halia central.

Haliacmon.note: Haliacmon is a river son of Tethys and Oceanus.

Halirrhothius.note: Ares kills Halirrhothius for violating or attempting to violate Alcippe.

Harpagos.note: Podarge is the mother of the supernatural foal Harpagos.

Harpinna.note: One tradition makes Harpinna the mother by Ares of Oenomaus.

Hecaerge.note: Hecaerge is Boreas's daughter in a Hyperborean genealogy.

Hector.note: Apollo aids Hector and preserves his corpse from damage.
Athena deceives Hector into standing and fighting Achilles.
Iris delivers Zeus’s instructions governing Hector’s return to battle.
Hector.date: late eighth or early seventh BCE

Hector.note: Zeus weighs Hector’s fate against Achilles’s before Hector’s death.

Hekate.note: Hemera and Hekate are co-recipients on the same inscribed altar.

Helen.note: Aphrodite approaches Helen disguised as an old woman.
Aphrodite threatens Helen and compels her to return to Paris's bed.
Helen identifies Castor and Polydeuces as her brothers.
The twins invade Attica, capture Aphidna, and recover Helen after her abduction.
The deified twins announce Helen's future cult, divine fate, and namesake island.
Disguised as Laodice, Iris summons Helen to view the armies.
Helen.date: late eighth or early seventh BCE

Helen.note: Nemesis conceives Helen after Zeus’s compelled union with her.
Nemesis lays the egg from which Helen hatches under Leda’s care.
The Rhamnous statue base presented Nemesis as Helen’s true mother.
One tradition makes Helen Zeus’s daughter by Leda.
The Cypria tradition makes Helen Zeus’s daughter by Nemesis.

Helicon.note: Pegasus strikes Helicon with his hoof and releases Hippocrene.
Pegasus stamps down personified Helicon when the mountain swells toward heaven.

Hellen.note: The Aeolian ancestor Aeolus is a son of Hellen.
Late genealogies make Hellen a son of Prometheus.

Hephaistos.note: Sacrificial offerings for Ploutos’ incubation are given to Hephaistos’ altar fire.
Some traditions make Hephaistos the joint child of Zeus and Hera.
Hephaistos intervenes in Zeus and Hera’s quarrel.
One early account has Zeus cast Hephaistos from heaven for aiding Hera.

Heptaporus.note: Heptaporus is a river son of Tethys and Oceanus.

Hermes Trismegistus.note: Hermes-Thoth syncretism produced the Graeco-Egyptian revelatory teacher Hermes Trismegistus.

Hermus.note: Hermus is a river son of Tethys and Oceanus.

Herophilos.note: A variant makes Herophilos the child of Aphrodite and Poseidon.

Herse.note: Ovid portrays Mercury desiring and seeking access to Herse.

Heryshaf.note: Greeks at Heracleopolis Magna equated Heracles with the Egyptian ram deity.

Hesperides.note: Roman catalogues make the Hesperides children of Erebus and Night.
Ladon and the Hesperides share responsibility for guarding the golden apples.
The Hesperides lament beside Ladon after Heracles kills him.
Nyx bears the Hesperides without a partner.
A marginal scholion makes the Hesperides children of Themis and Zeus.

Hesperis.note: Hesperis and Atlas are parents of seven Hesperides in Diodorus.

Hesperus.note: Hesperus leads Demeter to a chair beside Astraeus’s seat.
Diodorus makes Hesperus Atlas's brother and father-in-law.
Hesperus appears among the alternative parents of the Hesperides.

Hilaeira.myth: Marriage or abduction of the Leucippides
Hilaeira.note: One twin takes Hilaeira as wife, through marriage or abduction.

Himeros.note: Himeros accompanies Aphrodite from her birth.
Some later genealogies recast Aphrodite's companion Himeros as her son.
The Charites live and dance near Himeros on Olympus.
Eros and Himeros jointly attend Aphrodite after her sea-birth.
Eros and Himeros appear together as attendants of Aphrodite.
Himeros appears with Harmonia in the bridal scene.

Hippe.note: Variant dramatic and astronomical traditions name Hippe or related figures as Chiron's daughter.

Hippolyta.note: Hippolyta is assigned to Ares, often with Otrera as mother.
In one influential version, Hera provokes battle and Heracles kills Hippolyta.

Hippolytus.note: Aphrodite destroys Hippolytus for rejecting her honors.
Hippolytus devotes himself to Artemis and rejects Aphrodite and sexuality.
Artemis reveals the truth, reconciles him with Theseus, and establishes memorial rites.
Asclepius restores the dead Hippolytus, later concealed in Italy as Virbius.
Poseidon sends a sea-bull causing Hippolytus’ fatal chariot wreck.

Hippomenes.note: Venus gives Hippomenes three golden apples to win his race.
Venus incites sacrilegious intercourse and transforms Hippomenes into a lion.

Hippotas.note: Homer identifies Aeolus as the son or descendant of Hippotas.

Hopladamus.note: Rhea recruits Hopladamus and his Giants to protect her from Cronus.

Hora.note: Iris escorts Hersilia as she is transformed into the goddess Hora.

Horai.note: The Horai clothe and ornament Aphrodite for the judgment.
The Horai join Aphrodite in presenting Ariadne’s bridal crown.
The Horai are daughters of Zeus and Themis.

Horkos.note: The Erinyes attend Horkos’ birth on the fifth day.
Eris bears Horkos, the oath that punishes perjury.

Hundred-Handers.note: The Hundred-Handers are decisive allies of Zeus against Cronos’s faction.
The Cyclopes and Hundred-Handers are children of Gaia and Uranus.

Hundred-Handers.myth: Imprisonment and release of the Hundred-Handers
Hundred-Handers.note: The Hundred-Handers are imprisoned in Tartarus before Zeus releases them.
After defeating the Titans, the Hundred-Handers guard them at Tartarus.

Hunger.note: Demeter invokes personified Hunger to torment Erysichthon for violating her grove.
In Ovid’s version, Hunger carries out Ceres’ punishment of Erysichthon.

Hyacinthus.note: In a late variant, jealous Zephyrus causes Apollo’s discus to strike Hyacinthus.
Hyacinthus is Apollo's beloved youth in Amyclaean tradition.
Apollo accidentally kills Hyacinthus with a discus and mourns him.
Apollo causes a lament-marked flower to grow from Hyacinthus's blood.
Boreas loves Hyacinthus in a minority late variant.
The Horae and associated goddesses carry Hyacinthus to heaven.
A minority genealogy makes Clio the mother of Hyacinthus.
Zephyrus loves Hyacinthus, who rejects him in favor of Apollo.
Jealous Zephyrus redirects Apollo’s discus into Hyacinthus’ head.

Hyas.note: Hyas is Atlas's son whose death prompts the Hyades' mourning.

Hybris.myth: Hybris and Ate attend the third wine-bowl
Hybris.note: The third wine-bowl jointly brings Hybris and Ate, marking excessive drinking’s ruinous consequences.
Hyginus’s expanded genealogy makes Hybris a child of Erebus and Night.
The Gigantes’ destruction is associated with Hybris, personified arrogant violence.
A distinct learned Pan is described as the son of Hybris and Zeus.

Hydaspes.note: Oceanus addresses Tethys as mother while lamenting their threatened river child Hydaspes.
Urania removes Hymenaeus from the divinized river's supernatural flood.

Hydne.note: Glaucus loves Hydne, daughter of the diver Scyllias.

Hydra.note: Venom from the Hydra on Heracles' arrow makes Chiron's wound incurable.
Hydra venom on Heracles’ arrows kills Ladon, though the monsters never meet.
The Hydra is born to Typhaon and Echidna.

Hygieia.note: Hygieia is Asclepius' daughter and principal healing-family partner.
Asclepius and Hygieia receive joint cult and appear together in images.

Hymenaeus.note: Hymenaeus is named among Apollo's male beloveds.
Late resurrection catalogues name Hymenaeus among those restored by Asclepius.
Hymenaeus is repeatedly described as Urania's son or offspring.
Urania carries Hymenaeus through the air away from Hydaspes' flood.

Hymenaeus.myth: Globe offered in the kottabos contest
Hymenaeus.note: Hymenaeus possesses and offers a revolving starry globe made by Urania.

Hysminai.note: Eris bears the collective Hysminai without a named father.
The Hysminai advance beside the Keres in a battlefield description.

Iacchus.note: Dionysus is gradually assimilated to Eleusis’s torch-bearing procession figure.
Iacchus shares Eleusinian ritual space and representations with Plouton and Kore.

Ialmenus.note: Ialmenus is named among Ares’s sons in Greek genealogy.

Ianthe.note: Ianthe is an Oceanid daughter of Tethys and Oceanus.
Ianthe and Tyche belong to the company of Oceanid sisters.
Ianthe and Tyche gather flowers and play among Persephone’s Oceanid companions.

Iapetos.note: Iapetos and Cronos belong to the same generation of Titans.
Homer places Iapetos and Cronos together beyond sunlight and wind.
Iapetos and Themis are Titan children of Gaia and Ouranos.

Iasion.note: Demeter sleeps with Iasion in a thrice-ploughed field.
A later variant recasts their mutual union as Iasion’s attempted violation.
Ploutos is born from Iasion’s union with Demeter in Crete.

Iaso.note: Iaso is Asclepius' daughter and personification of recovery.
Iaso accompanies Asclepius in healing-family worship and reliefs.

Iasus.note: Argus and Ismene are the parents of Iasus.

Icelos.note: Icelos is Morpheus’s brother and the specialist in animal dream-forms.
Icelos, called Phobetor by mortals, is a dream-son specializing in animal forms.

Icelos/Phobetor.note: Ovid names Icelos, called Phobetor by mortals, among Somnus’s dream-sons.

Ichnaea.note: Ichnaea and Amphitrite attend Leto’s labor together.

Ida.note: Rhea entrusts infant Zeus to the nymph Ida.

Idaean Heracles.note: Later Greeks assimilated Heracles to an Idaean Dactyl credited with athletic foundations.

Idas.note: Idas fights the twins and mortally wounds Castor before Zeus destroys him.

Idmon.note: Some genealogies make Idmon a son of Apollo and Cyrene.

Ieoud.note: Ieoud is Cronos’s only son in Philo’s catastrophe-sacrifice narrative.
During a catastrophe, Cronos sacrifices his only son Ieoud.

Illyrius.note: Later western tradition makes Harmonia mother of the Illyrian ancestor-eponym.
Appian names Illyrius as a son of Polyphemus and Galatea.

Impietas.note: Juno proposes summoning Discordia together with Impietas from the underworld.

Inachus.note: Genealogical scholarship alternatively makes Argus a son of Inachus.
Inachus is named as a son of Tethys and Oceanus.

Ino.note: Amphitrite rises radiantly to receive or witness Ino’s entry into the sea.
Ino receives and nurses the newborn Dionysus in one tradition.
Harmonia is mother of Ino, who is later divinized as Leucothea.
Nonnus assimilates divinized Ino to the Nereids’ marine community.
The Thalamian oracle is called Ino's despite containing Pasiphae's image.
Poseidon wrecks Odysseus while Ino helps the hero survive.

Inuus.note: Roman interpretation sometimes equated the Italian god Inuus with Pan.

Invidia.note: Hyginus lists the personification Invidia among Pallas and Styx’s offspring.
Hyginus’s corrupt expanded genealogy lists Invidia among Styx’s offspring.

Io.note: Through his son Iasus, Argus is made Io’s grandfather.
Argus guards, confines, drives, and watches Io after her bovine transformation.
Io is Dionysus’s mother in a marginal genealogy.

Io.myth: Io’s story decorates Europa’s golden basket
Io.note: Europa carries Io’s former basket, whose images parallel their transformations and transport through Zeus’s desire.
Hera guards Io through Argus and sends a gadfly to drive her wandering.
Some variants make Hera responsible for transforming Io into a cow.
Hermes frees Io from Argus's guardianship on Zeus's command.
Prometheus recounts Io's wanderings and foretells liberation by her descendant Heracles.
Zeus desires Io, prompting Hera’s hostility and Io’s bovine wandering.

Iolaus.note: Hebe and Heracles appear as stars before aged Iolaus becomes young.
Hebe directly restores Iolaus' youthful years as an exceptional favor.

Iphigenia.note: Artemis substitutes a deer for Iphigenia and transports her to Tauris.
Artemis appoints the rescued Iphigenia as her priestess in Tauris.
A disputed Hesiodic tradition says Iphigenia became, or is, Hecate.

Iphimedeia.note: Iphimedeia says she lay with Poseidon and bore the Aloadae.

Ismene.note: Cercops reportedly names Ismene as a parent of Argus.
Argus takes Ismene, daughter of Asopus, as his consort.

Ismenian dragon.note: A sacred dragon belonging to Ares guards his spring at Thebes.

Ister.note: Ister is named among Oceanus's river sons.
Ister is a river son of Tethys and Oceanus.

Iynx.note: Varying later genealogies sometimes make Iynx Pan’s child.

Japheth.note: Early-modern mythographers equated Iapetus with Noah's son Japheth.

Jason.note: Chiron protects, raises, and educates Jason away from Pelias before his return.
Circe ritually purifies Jason of blood guilt, then expels him from her home.
The twins join Jason's crew for the voyage of the Argo.
Eros induces Medea's love so that she will help Jason survive.
After Glaucus' apotheosis, he remains visible only to Jason.
Hecate receives Jason's pit sacrifice and manifests amid serpents and barking dogs.
Jason carries Hera, disguised as an old woman, across the flooded Anauros.
Hera becomes Jason's divine patron and helps him obtain the Golden Fleece.
Iris helps arrange Jason’s consequential meeting with Medea.

Jocastus.note: Jocastus is one of Aeolus' six colonizing sons.

Jupiter Dolichenus.note: Victoria crowns or accompanies Jupiter Dolichenus in imperial iconographic programs.

Jupiter’s eagle.note: Jupiter’s eagle negotiates passage and retrieves Styx water for Psyche.

Kabeiroi.note: Some Hellenistic and Roman cult environments associate or equate the Dioscuri with the Kabeiroi.

Kakasbos.note: Club-bearing Heracles partially converged with the mounted Anatolian god Kakasbos.

Kakia.note: Kakia offers Heracles an easy life devoted to pleasure.

Kalligeneia.note: Kalligeneia and Ploutos are invoked together in the women’s festival prayer.

Kallisto.note: Kallisto is listed among Zeus’s important partners and bears Arkas.

Ker.note: Ker and Atropos are siblings under Hesiod's Night genealogy.
Eris and destructive Ker occupy the same battle scene.
Ker and Nemesis are fatherless children of Nyx.
Nyx bears Ker without a partner.
Ker and Thanatos belong to Nyx's fatherless brood.

Keto.note: Keto is Medusa’s mother in the Hesiodic marine-monster genealogy.

Koios.note: Koios and Themis are Titan children of Gaia and Ouranos.

Kotys.note: Hecate is contextually equated with Kotys in cultic or magical interpretation.

Kouretes.note: The Kouretes clash weapons to conceal the infant Zeus’s cries.

Kourotrophos.note: Kourotrophos and Ploutos are invoked together in the women’s festival prayer.

Kratos.note: Kratos is Nike’s sibling, born to Pallas and Styx.

Kratos.date: late eighth or early seventh century BCE

Kratos.note: Kratos supervises the chaining and demands strict execution of Zeus's sentence.
Kratos is the son of Styx and Pallas.
Styx brings Kratos to Zeus, beside whom he remains.

Krios.note: Krios and Themis are Titan children of Gaia and Ouranos.

Kronos.note: Kronos casts Ouranos's genitals into the sea, indirectly generating Aphrodite.
Hesiod names Kronos as Demeter’s father.
Kronos belongs to the royal succession descended from Phanes.
Modern comparisons linked Talos’s heated embrace with reported Sardinian or Carthaginian sacrifice to Kronos.
Kronos and Themis are Titan children of Gaia and Ouranos.
Kronos is Zeus’s father in the dominant Hesiodic genealogy.
Zeus escapes swallowing, compels Kronos to release his siblings, and overthrows him.

Kydoimos.note: Eris and Kydoimos occupy the same battle scene on Achilles' shield.
Kydoimos mingles with Eris and a destructive Kēr amid battle.

Kyknos.note: Kyknos plans to build Phobos a temple from travelers’ skulls.

Labor.note: Roman catalogues make Toil a child of Erebus and Night.
Labor accompanies Penia’s antagonistic entourage and intimidates Ploutos.

Lacus.note: Hyginus lists the personified Lakes among Pallas and Styx’s offspring.
Hyginus’s corrupt expanded genealogy lists Lacus among Styx’s offspring.

Laelaps.myth: Marvelous protections for Europa’s Cretan household
Laelaps.note: A dispersed tradition traces the infallible hunting dog through Europa to Minos.

Laestrygonians.note: The monstrous Laestrygonians are compared with the Gigantes rather than ordinary men.

Lake Tritonis.note: The Auseans call Athena the daughter of Poseidon and personified Lake Tritonis.

Lamia.note: Scylla is reportedly named as Lamia's daughter.

Lampetie.note: Lampetie is Helios's daughter by Neaera.
Lampetie guards Helios's herds and reports their slaughter.

Lampē.note: Later sources name Lampē or Lampus as one of Eos's shining chariot horses.

Laodameia.note: Laodameia is listed among Zeus’s important partners.

Latinus.note: Calypso bears Latinus to Odysseus in an imperial mythographic genealogy.
Latinus is named as a son of Circe and Odysseus.
Hyginus alternatively makes Latinus the son of Circe and Telemachus.

Latramys.note: Variant genealogical compilations list Latramys as Ariadne’s child.

Leda.note: Leda bears both twins and possesses local heroic and cultic status.
Zeus mates with Leda in swan form in one tradition.

Lemnian women.note: Aphrodite afflicts the neglectful Lemnian women with a repellent odor.

Leo.myth: The slain lion becomes the constellation Leo
Leo.note: Catasteristic tradition identifies the terrestrial Nemean Lion with Leo.

Lethe.note: Lethe is Dionysus’s mother in a marginal genealogy.
Eris bears Lethe without a named father.
The hymn names Lethe as Hypnos’s sister.
Mnemosyne’s water is paired and functionally contrasted with Lethe’s water.

Leucippe.note: Leucippe and Tyche belong to the company of Oceanid sisters.
Leucippe and Tyche gather flowers and play among Persephone’s Oceanid companions.

Leucippus.note: Jealous Apollo exposes Leucippus's disguise, leading Daphne's companions to kill him.

Leuconoe.note: Leuconoe is one variant mother of Apollo's son Philammon.

Leucothea.note: Calypso learns by letter that Leucothea saved Odysseus after his departure.

Leucothoe.note: Helios enters disguised as Leucothoe's mother, reveals himself, and sleeps with her.
Unable to revive the buried Leucothoe, Helios transforms or sanctifies her as frankincense.

Leuke.note: Pluto abducts the Oceanid Leuke in a late-antique account.
After Leuke’s death, Pluto changes her into Elysium’s white poplar.

Libya.note: Later traditions name Libya as a partner of Iapetus.

Libyan serpents.note: Drops of blood from Medusa’s severed head generate Libya’s poisonous serpents.

Limos.note: Eris bears Limos without a named father.

Linus.note: Some genealogies make Linus a son of Apollo and a Muse.
Calliope or another Muse is named as Linus's mother.
Urania bears Linus with Amphimarus in the Heliconian genealogy.
Urania is Linus' mother, with Apollo identified as father.
A learned alternative makes Urania and Hermes the parents of Linus.

Liparus.note: Aeolus marries Liparus' daughter, succeeds him, and grants him territory.

Litai.myth: The Litai follow and remedy Ate
Litai.note: The slow Litai pursue swift Ate, healing her damage or requesting her punishment of the unreceptive.

Livia Augusta.note: Rhamnous closely associated Nemesis with the deified empress without universal identification.

Logoi.note: Eris bears the collective Logoi without a named father.

Lotis.note: Priapus attempts to assault sleeping Lotis, but an ass awakens her.
Lotis becomes a lotus tree while fleeing Priapus.

Loxo.note: Loxo is Boreas's daughter in a Hyperborean genealogy.

Lycaon.note: Lycaon is named among Ares’s children in varying genealogical traditions.

Lycurgus.note: Asclepius raises Lycurgus with Capaneus in an early variant.
Lycurgus is Boreas's son by an unnamed mother.
Disguised as Ares, Iris deceives and incites Lycurgus against Dionysus.

Lycus.note: Late sources make Lycus a son of Prometheus and Celaeno.

Lykaon.note: Later traditions have Zeus kill, strike, or transform Lykaon after a cannibalistic test.

Lymphae.note: Roman freshwater powers became linguistically and conceptually associated with Greek nymphs.

Lynceus.note: Polydeuces kills Lynceus after Lynceus helps ambush and mortally wound Castor.
