Castor fights Lynceus in a formal duel during the Leucippid conflict.

Lyncus.note: Demeter transforms Lyncus into a lynx for plotting against Triptolemus.

Lysidice.note: Tzetzes names Lysidice among Aeolus' twelve intermarried children.

Lyssa.note: Hera sends Lyssa through Iris to drive Heracles mad.
Lyssa reluctantly inflicts the madness that destroys Heracles’ household.
Lyssa is the daughter of Nyx and Uranus.

Ma.note: Strabo identifies the Cappadocian goddess Ma as Enyo through Greek interpretatio.

Macar.note: Later catalogues attribute Macar to Helios.

Macareus.note: Tragic and Roman tradition makes Macareus a son of Aeolus.
Tzetzes includes Macareus among the named children of Homeric Aeolus.

Macaria.note: The Suda alone clearly identifies Macaria as Hades’ daughter.

Machai.note: Eris bears the collective Machai without a named father.

Machaon.note: Machaon inherits knowledge of Chiron's medicinal drugs through his father Asclepius.
Hemera and Machaon are co-recipients on the same inscribed altar.

Maeander.note: Maeander is named among Oceanus's river sons.
Maeander is a river son of Tethys and Oceanus.

Maenads.note: Maenads form Dionysus’s ecstatic female retinue and enact his rites.
Nymphs and maenads jointly accompany Dionysus in processions.

Maera.note: Sporadic genealogical traditions count Maera among Atlas's daughters.

Magnes.note: Magnes is listed among the sons of Aeolus and Enarete.

Maia.note: Maia, mother of Hermes, is a daughter of Atlas.
Maia, daughter of Atlas, gives birth to Hermes in Cyllene.

Maia.myth: Maia rebukes the newborn cattle thief
Maia.note: Maia rebukes Hermes after he returns from stealing Apollo's cattle.
Zeus secretly visits Maia, who bears Hermes.

Manto.note: Manto is named as Apollo's partner and mother of Mopsus.

Maponus.note: Roman provincial inscriptions interpretively pair Apollo with Maponus.

Marsyas.note: Apollo defeats Marsyas in a contest between lyre and aulos.
After winning, Apollo hangs, flays, and kills Marsyas.
Athena discards her aulos, which Marsyas takes up before challenging Apollo.

Maḥrem.note: Greek royal inscriptions translate the Aksumite dynastic god Maḥrem as Ares.

Medea.myth: Titane priests chant Medea’s wind charms
Medea.note: Medea’s reported charms are sung in a regional rite to quiet the winds.
Through Eros's arrow, Aphrodite induces Medea's passion.
Circe recognizes Medea as her niece, purifies her, then expels her.
Diodorus alternatively makes Medea and Circe daughters of Hecate and Aeëtes.
Eros shoots Medea, igniting the desire that leads her to aid Jason.
Diodorus's Euhemeristic genealogy makes Medea Hecate's daughter.
Hecate teaches Medea the handling of magical herbs and drugs.
Medea is Helios's granddaughter through Aeetes.
Helios supplies Medea a dragon-drawn chariot for her escape.
Iris helps arrange Medea’s meeting with Jason.
Selene exults that Aphrodite has afflicted Medea with similar love-madness.

Medea.myth: Medea magically causes Talos’s fatal fall
Medea.note: Medea’s hostile magic bewilders Talos, who wounds his ankle and loses his ichor.

Medea.myth: Medea drives Talos mad with drugs
Medea.note: One variant says Medea destroys Talos by inducing madness with drugs.
Medea falsely promises immortality so she can remove Talos’s bronze nail.
Medea removes the nail sealing Talos’s vein, causing his life-giving ichor to drain.
Thetis saves Medea’s vessel because Hera predicts Medea will marry Achilles.
A late tradition places Thetis and Medea in a beauty contest.

Megaera.note: Hypnos keeps Zeus asleep while Hera deploys Megaera against Dionysus.

Megaira.note: Megaira is accumulated among Hecate's magical names and functions.

Melaina.note: Melaina is one variant mother of Apollo's son Delphus.

Melanippe.note: Melanippe is assigned to Ares among the Amazon queens.
Poseidon fathers Aeolus and Boeotus with Melanippe.

Melanippus.note: Triton is Melanippus’s maternal grandfather through Triteia.

Meleager.note: A minority genealogical tradition makes Meleager a son of Ares.
Atropos declares Meleager will live only while the hearth-brand remains unconsumed.
The Fates bind infant Meleager's lifespan to an unconsumed firebrand.
The Sisters prophesy that Meleager will live while the brand survives.

Meliae.note: Gaia receives Uranus’s blood and bears the Meliae.
The Meliae and Gigantes are co-born from Uranus’s fallen blood.
The Meliae arise when Uranus's blood falls upon Gaia.

Meliai.note: Gaia bears the Erinyes and Meliai from Uranus’ blood.

Melian nymphs.note: They arise indirectly when blood from Cronos’s assault falls upon Gaia.

Melicertes/Palaemon.myth: Leap into the sea for Melicertes
Melicertes/Palaemon.note: Glaucus enters the sea because of his love for Melicertes.
Nicanor explicitly says that Melicertes' name was changed to Glaucus.
Glaucus and Palaemon jointly help propel Aeneas' fleet.

Melinoe.note: Persephone bears the nocturnal goddess Melinoe after Zeus approaches her disguised as Pluto.

Melobosis.note: Melobosis and Tyche belong to the company of Oceanid sisters.
Melobosis and Tyche gather flowers and play among Persephone’s Oceanid companions.

Melpomene.note: Melpomene is a daughter of Mnemosyne and Zeus.
Melpomene is their mother by Achelous in two mythographic accounts.
Melpomene and Urania are daughters of Zeus and Mnemosyne.

Memnon.note: Memnon is the heroic son of Eos and Tithonus.
Eos secures posthumous immortality for Memnon by petitioning Zeus.
Eos mourns and carries her dead son after Achilles kills him.
Hemera is called Memnon’s mother in traditions otherwise assigning maternity to Eos.

Mene.note: Later poetry and magic use Mene as a name or aspect of Selene.

Menelaus.note: Iris informs Menelaus that Helen has departed with Paris.

Menoetes.note: Menoetes warns Geryon about Heracles and urges consideration of his parents.

Mercy.note: Hyginus lists Mercy among Nox's expanded offspring.

Merope.note: Merope is one of Atlas and Pleione's seven daughters.

Metameleia.note: Later scholia attach the personification of Regret to Epimetheus as his daughter.

Midday.note: Images of Day and Midday appear together among cosmic personifications.

Mimas.note: Ares kills the Giant Mimas during the gods’ war against the Giants.
Hephaestus kills the Giant Mimas with molten iron or metal.

Minos.note: Ariadne is consistently identified as Minos’ daughter.
Later systems place Minos among the judges in Hades’ realm.
Zeus fathers Minos with Europa after carrying her to Crete.

Minthe.note: One variant makes Demeter transform Minthe into mint; another assigns the act to Persephone.
Regional tradition describes the nymph Minthe as Hades’ concubine.

Misenus.note: Jealous of Misenus’s shell-playing challenge, Triton seizes and drowns him.

Miseria.note: Roman catalogues make Misery a child of Erebus and Night.

Mnasinous.note: Mnasinous is represented at Argos as a son of the twins.

Moirai.note: Ocyrhoe predicts the Fates will cut Chiron's thread once an immortal may die.
The Moirai persuade the grieving, enraged Demeter to leave her cave and relent.
The Moirai kill Agrius with bronze clubs.
The Moirai kill Thoon with bronze clubs.
The Fates negotiate mortal death independently of Hades’ underworld sovereignty.
Hesiod makes the Horae and Moirai sibling groups born to Zeus and Themis.
They accompany the Moirai and Charites during Persephone's return.
The Moirai and Keres are listed together among Nyx's daughters.
Nyx bears the Moirai without a partner.
A Byzantine variant makes Nyx and Cronus parents of the Moirai.
Tyche is interpreted as one of the Fates and more powerful than her sisters.
Hesiod makes the Moirai daughters of Zeus and Themis.
Homeric fate can constrain Zeus, who weighs or accepts destined deaths.

Molossus.note: Molossus, son of Neoptolemus and Andromache, is Thetis’s great-grandson.

Molus.note: Molus is a son of Ares and Demonice in Apollodoran genealogy.

Momos.note: Momos and Atropos are siblings under Hesiod's Night genealogy.
Momos and Nemesis are fatherless children of Nyx.
Momos and Thanatos belong to Nyx's fatherless brood.

Moritasgus.note: Healing inscriptions compound Apollo's name with the local god Moritasgus.

Moros.note: Moros and Atropos are siblings under Hesiod's Night genealogy.
Eris appears with Moros amid Trojan-war slaughter.
Moros and the Keres belong to Nyx's brood of destructive powers.

Moros.myth: Moros rejoices with Keres in battle
Moros.note: Moros rejoices alongside the Keres and Eris amid battle.
Moros is Lachesis's sibling under Hesiod's genealogy from Nyx.
Hesiod makes Moros and Momus fatherless children of Nyx.
Moros and Nemesis are fatherless children of Nyx.
Nyx bears Moros without a partner.
Moros and Thanatos belong to Nyx's fatherless brood.

Mors.note: Latin authors translate or interpret Greek Thanatos as the personified Mors.

Morta.note: Roman interpretive tradition conventionally equates Atropos with Morta.

Mutunus Tutunus.note: Late Roman and Christian authors compare or equate the Roman phallic god with Priapus.

Mycene.note: A genealogical branch makes Mycene the mother of Argus.

Mylitta.note: Herodotus interprets Mylitta through the Greek category of Aphrodite.

Myrtilus.note: Hermes fathers Myrtilus; the mother's identity varies among traditions.

Naiads.myth: Childhood in the caves of Ida
Naiads.note: Naiads nurse the young Hermaphroditus in the caves of Ida.

Narcissus.note: Echo desires Narcissus, who rejects her, and she wastes away.

Natio.note: Learned sources occasionally offer the Roman birth personification Natio as Eileithyia's counterpart.

Nauplius.note: Later mythography makes Nauplius the son of Poseidon and Amymone.

Nausithous.note: Hyginus names Nausithous as a son of Circe and Odysseus.

Naïs.note: The nymph Naïs bears Glaucus to Poseidon.

Neaera.note: Neaera bears Helios's divine cattle-herding daughters.
The nymphs Phaethusa and Lampetie are daughters of Neaera and Helios.

Neda.note: Rhea entrusts infant Zeus to Neda, who washes or carries him.

Neikea.note: Eris bears the collective Neikea without a named father.

Nemea.note: Scholia make Nemea a daughter of Zeus and Selene.

Nemertes.note: Nemertes is a daughter of Nereus and Doris.
Nemertes possesses the same truthful or unerring nature as Nereus.

Neoptolemus.note: Neoptolemus, son of Achilles, is Thetis’s grandson.
Appearing as deus ex machina, Thetis directs the burial of her grandson.

Nephelai.myth: Invocation of Aether and the Clouds
Nephelai.note: Aether is invoked within the Clouds' celestial setting.
A later scholastic tradition calls Aether father of the Clouds.

Nerites.note: A local or later tradition names Nerites as Aphrodite's lover.
Aelian makes Nerites another child of Nereus and Doris.
Aelian adds Nerites as a son of Nereus and Doris.

Nessus.note: Heracles shoots Nessus with a Hydra-poisoned arrow after the centaur attacks Deianira.
Nessus’s false love-charm instructions ultimately cause Heracles’ mortal agony.
Nessus is killed by an arrow carrying the Hydra's venom.
Nessus is a river son of Tethys and Oceanus.

Nethuns.note: The Etruscan water-god adopts Poseidon-like trident imagery through assimilation.

Night.note: Chaos and ancient Night inhabit the turbulent abyss outside the created world.
The Erinyes call Night their mother; no father is named.
Night lays the egg in Erebus from which golden-winged Eros hatches.
Hesiod makes the Hesperides children of Night.
Orphic Rhapsodic fragments place Night before Uranus in divine kingship.

Nile.note: Nile is named among Oceanus's river sons.
Nile is a river son of Tethys and Oceanus.

Niobe.note: Apollo kills Niobe's sons after she boasts against Leto.
Artemis kills Niobe’s daughters after Niobe boasts against Leto.
Niobe claims the Atlantid Dione as her mother, making Atlas her ancestor.
Niobe is listed among Zeus’s important partners.

Nona.note: Later comparative convention aligns the Roman Nona with Clotho.

Norax.note: Geryon is Norax's maternal grandfather through his daughter Erytheia.

Nox.note: A learned Latin genealogy makes corresponding destructive abstractions children of Nox and Erebus.
Hyginus makes Fate, Destruction, and related abstractions offspring of Nox and Erebus.
Roman Nox is the regular Latin translation-equivalent of Greek Nyx.

Nychie.note: Phoibiē and Nychie occupy two angles of the triple magical figure.

Ocean.note: An Oceanid named Calypso is catalogued as Ocean and Tethys's daughter.
Geryon is Ocean's maternal grandson through Callirhoe.
Menoetius is Ocean’s grandson through his Oceanid mother.
Ocean.date: late eighth century BCE–second century CE

Ocean.note: Pausanias gives Ocean as Nemesis’s father at Rhamnous.
Ocean advises submission and offers to intercede with Zeus, but Prometheus refuses.

Oceanids.note: Sixty young Oceanids become Artemis’ attendants and chorus.
The Oceanids accompany Persephone while she gathers flowers before Hades abducts her.
Oceanus and Tethys generate three thousand divine daughters.
His daughters leave their father's house and remain beside bound Prometheus.
Persephone gathers meadow flowers with a named company of Oceanid nymphs.
The Oceanids lament with Prometheus and remain beside him during the catastrophe.
Tethys bears three thousand Oceanid daughters to Oceanus.

Oceanos.note: Oceanos and Themis are Titan children of Gaia and Ouranos.

Ochimus.note: Ochimus is listed among Helios's Rhodian sons.

Ocyrhoe.note: Ocyrhoe is the prophetic daughter of Chiron and Chariclo.

Ocyrhoe.myth: Ocyrhoe prophesies Chiron's wound and death
Ocyrhoe.note: His daughter foretells his incurable wound; Chiron later appeals helplessly when she becomes a mare.

Ocyrrhoe.note: Ocyrrhoe and Tyche are daughters of Oceanus and Tethys.
Ocyrrhoe and Tyche gather flowers and play among Persephone’s Oceanid companions.

Odysseus.note: Aeolus gives Odysseus an oxhide container holding the adverse winds.
Aeolus aids Odysseus once but refuses renewed help after his return.
Athena plans, disguises, protects, and directs Odysseus throughout his return.
Athena’s safeguard is stolen from Troy by Odysseus and Diomedes.
Calypso makes the unwilling Odysseus her sexual partner and desires him as husband.
Calypso receives, feeds, and saves Odysseus after he reaches Ogygia alone.
Calypso prevents Odysseus from departing and tries to make him forget Ithaca.
She offers immortality, then supplies tools, clothing, provisions, wind, and sailing guidance.
Calypso unites with Odysseus and bears Nausithous and Nausinous.
Calypso sleeps with Odysseus and bears Latinus during a five-year stay.
The dead Odysseus writes that he regrets rejecting Calypso and hopes to return.
A late mythographic account says Calypso killed herself from love for Ulysses.
Immune to her drug, Odysseus threatens Circe until she swears against harming him.
Circe becomes Odysseus’s lover and hosts him and his crew for a year.
Circe teaches Odysseus the route, rites, and sacrifices for consulting Tiresias.
Circe warns Odysseus about the Sirens, Scylla, Charybdis, and Helios’s cattle.
Circe provides the stingray-spine spear with which Telegonus accidentally kills Odysseus.
Polyphemus traps Odysseus's party and eats companions before Odysseus blinds him.
Odysseus calls himself Nobody, causing Polyphemus's neighbors to disregard his cries.
Odysseus and his survivors escape Polyphemus's cave concealed beneath sheep.

Odysseus.myth: The cave, blinding, escape, and curse
Odysseus.note: Polyphemus eats Odysseus’s men before Odysseus blinds and escapes him.

Odysseus.myth: Odysseus uses wine and the Nobody name-trick
Odysseus.note: Odysseus intoxicates him, gives the name Nobody, and escapes beneath rams.
Poseidon answers Polyphemus’ curse with storms, losses, and delayed homecoming.
Odysseus must establish Poseidon’s inland cult and sacrifice after returning home.
Their song tempts him, but binding and deafened sailors carry him safely past.
Later traditions make his safe passage fulfill the prophecy causing their deaths.
Zeus destroys Odysseus’s ship after his crew kill Helios’s cattle.

Odysseus’s crew.note: Circe drugs twenty-two sailors and changes their bodies into swine.
Circe reverses the transformation, restoring the sailors younger and more handsome.

Oeagrus.note: Oeagrus fathers Orpheus with Calliope in a common genealogy.

Oeneis.note: A late genealogical variant names Oeneis as Pan’s mother.

Oenoe.note: Oenoe and Rhea jointly hold infant Zeus in a Tegean altar scene.

Oenomaus.note: Some traditions make Oenomaus Ares’s son, with Harpinna or Sterope as mother.

Oenopion.note: Some traditions make Oenopion Ariadne’s son by Dionysus.
Oenopion is attributed to Dionysus and Ariadne.

Oileus.note: One bird launches a sharp feather that wounds Oileus in the shoulder.

Oizys.note: Oizys and Atropos are siblings under Hesiod's Night genealogy.
Hesiod names Oizys and Momus among Nyx's fatherless offspring.
Oizys and Nemesis are fatherless children of Nyx.
Nyx bears Oizys without a partner.
Oizys and Thanatos belong to Nyx's fatherless brood.

Olenus.note: Hyginus assigns Olenus to Vulcan as his son.

Oneiros.note: Oneiros and Hypnos Epidotēs jointly put a lion to sleep.
Modern scholars sometimes equate Morpheus with Homer’s unnamed impersonating Dream.

Ophion.note: Cronos and Rhea displace Ophion from rule and cast him into Ocean.
Defeated Ophion is expelled into Oceanus, called Ogenos in variant material.
Rhea joins Cronus in displacing Ophion and Eurynome from rule.

Ophioneus.note: Chronos leads the opposing army and defeats Ophioneus under agreed contest terms.
Ophioneus.source: Pherecydes via Celsus and Maximus of Tyre

Ophioneus’ divine followers.note: Chronos’ army defeats Ophioneus’ followers, who fall into Ogenos.
Ophioneus’ divine followers.source: Pherecydes via Celsus and Maximus of Tyre

Orcus.note: Roman literature later freely equates Orcus with Dis, Pluto, or the underworld.

Oreithyia.note: Boreas carries Oreithyia from Attica to Thrace and makes her his wife.
Oreithyia becomes Boreas's wife in the dominant Athenian genealogy.
Boreas abducts Oreithyia and carries her from Attica to Thrace.
Athenians invoke Boreas and Oreithyia together against Persian ships.

Orestes.note: Athena establishes a court, judges Orestes, and votes for his acquittal.

Orion.note: Artemis kills Orion when he attempts to rape her.
Artemis kills Orion because he assaults the Hyperborean maiden Opis.

Orion.myth: Apollo tricks Artemis into shooting Orion
Orion.note: Deceived by Apollo, Artemis shoots the distant Orion.
Artemis kills Orion on Ortygia after Eos abducts him.
Eos chooses or carries off Orion as a mortal lover.
Earth produces Orion from a buried hide wetted by three gods.
Gaia sends a scorpion against Orion in some accounts.

Ornis.note: Mnaseas makes Ornis, whose name means Bird, their mother.

Orontes.note: The river god swims beneath Antioch’s seated Tyche as a topographical emblem.

Orseis.note: The nymph Orseis is mother of the Aeolian ancestor Aeolus.

Orthanes.note: Strabo describes the Attic ithyphallic Orthanes as resembling Priapus.

Other Titans.note: Cronos belongs to the sibling generation collectively called the Titans.
Cronos’s Titan faction collectively fights the Olympian coalition.

Otrera.note: Later mythography commonly pairs Otrera with Ares as mother of Amazon queens.

Otus.note: Otus and Ephialtes bind Ares inside a bronze jar for thirteen months.
As a deer, Artemis runs between the brothers, causing mutual slaughter.
Otus institutes sacrifice to Melete, Mneme, and Aoide on Helicon.
Poseidon fathers the giant Otus with Iphimedeia.

Ouranos.note: The lost Titanomachy makes Ouranos a son of Aether.
Cornutus allegorically equates or closely assimilates Aether and Ouranos.
Aphrodite forms around Ouranos's severed genitals in sea foam.
Late Orphic material makes Ouranos a parent of the Moirai.
Ouranos is Cronos’s father in the principal Hesiodic genealogy.
Cronos ambushes, castrates, and overthrows his father with Gaia’s sickle.
Ouranos and Gaia warn that Cronos will be overcome by his own son.
Ouranos arises after Eros initiates the cosmic mingling of things.
Dies and Aether are named as the parents of Caelus.
Caelum is born to Aether and Dies.
Images of Day and Heaven appear together in Antiochus IV’s procession.
Hesiod names Ouranos as Themis’s father.
Ouranos is Zeus’s grandfather in Hesiod’s genealogy.
Ouranos joins Gaia in warning Rhea and supplying succession knowledge.

Ourea.note: Gaia produces the Mountains without a mate.

Oxylus.note: Some traditions make Oxylus the son of Ares and Protogeneia.

Ozomene.note: Ozomene replaces Electra as Iris’s mother in a Roman mythographic variant.

Paean.note: The initially independent healing divinity becomes absorbed as Apollo's healing title.

Paeon.note: At Zeus’s command, Paeon heals Ares’s divine wound.
The originally distinct divine healer's name later becomes an epithet of Asclepius.
Paeon heals Ares before Hebe washes and dresses him.

Paieon.note: Paieon heals Hades on Olympus after Heracles wounds him.

Paion.note: In Pherecydes's genealogy, Hecate's father Aristaeus is Paion's son.

Palaemon.note: A Corinthian cult group places Palaemon on a dolphin beside Amphitrite and Poseidon.

Palaemonius.note: Some sources explain the Argonaut Palaemonius's lameness through descent from Hephaestus.

Palici.note: A Sicilian variant makes the Palici children of Hephaestus and Aetna.

Pallas son of Megamedes.note: Pallas is named as Selene’s father in a conflicting genealogy.

Panacea.note: Panacea is Asclepius' daughter, personifying all-cure.
Asclepius and Panacea are jointly invoked as witnesses of the oath.

Panakeia.note: Panakeia covers Ploutos’ face while Asklepios’ snakes heal his eyes.

Pandia.note: Selene bears Pandia after union with Zeus.

Pandion.note: Boreas is variously named as Pandion’s grandfather through Cleopatra.

Pandora.note: Athena teaches Pandora weaving and helps adorn her.
The Charites adorn Pandora with golden necklaces, enhancing her dangerous beauty.
Epimetheus accepts Pandora despite Prometheus's warning and recognizes the harm afterward.
Later mythographers explicitly make Pandora the wife of Epimetheus.

Pandora.myth: Variant opening of the jar of evils
Pandora.note: Against the dominant Pandora-opening account, some said Epimetheus opened the jar after receiving her.
Hephaestus mixes earth and water and gives Pandora a maiden's form and voice.
Hermes contributes deceitful speech, lies, and a thievish disposition to Pandora.
The Horae crown the newly fashioned Pandora with spring flowers.
Zeus sends Pandora to humanity as retaliation for Prometheus's theft of fire.
Zeus commands the gods to construct Pandora as punishment connected with fire.

Panopea.note: Glaucus and Panopea jointly help drive Aeneas' ships onward.
Panopea is one of the Nereids fathered by Nereus.

Parammon.note: Parammon and Themis are invoked together in a Greco-Egyptian detection spell.

Parcae.note: Roman catalogues make the Fates children of Erebus and Night.

Paris.note: Paris awards Aphrodite victory after she promises him Helen.
Aphrodite promises Paris the most beautiful woman, Helen.
Aphrodite removes Paris from his duel with Menelaus.
Apollo assists Paris in killing Achilles in post-Homeric tradition.
Paris judges Aphrodite more beautiful than Hera and Athena.
Nereus stills the wind and foretells Paris' defeat and Troy's destruction.

Parthenius.note: Parthenius is a river son of Tethys and Oceanus.

Parthenope.note: A marginal genealogy makes Parthenope Europa’s mother.

Pasithea.note: Hera promises the desired Pasithea to Hypnos as his wife.
Pasithea and Thanatos occupy the same expanded Sarpedon iconographic program.

Patroclus.note: Apollo deceives or strikes Patroclus, strips his armor, and enables his death.
Boreas drives the fire throughout the night at Patroclus's funeral pyre.
Patroclus receives medical knowledge indirectly through Achilles, who learned it from Chiron.
Thetis preserves Patroclus’s body from decay using ambrosia and nectar.

Peiras.note: Epimenides reportedly made the otherwise obscure Peiras Echidna’s father.
A fragmentary regional genealogy makes Peiras Styx’s mate.

Peisidice.note: Peisidice is listed among the daughters of Aeolus and Enarete.

Peitho.note: Peitho recurrently accompanies Aphrodite in courtship and civic concord.
An individual late or local genealogy assigns Peitho to Aphrodite.
Aeschylus metaphorically calls ruinous Peitho the child of designing Ate.
The Charites and Peitho together place golden necklaces on Pandora.
Peitho appears beside Eros and Aphrodite in literary and visual configurations.
Peitho guides and persuades Harmonia during Cadmus' courtship.
Peitho accompanies Harmonia during her bridal preparation.
Later genealogies list Peitho as Hermes's lover or a mother by him.
Peitho is an Oceanid daughter of Tethys and Oceanus.
Peitho stands apart from Thanatos, who cannot be influenced by gifts or prayer.

Peleus.note: Atropos participates among the Parcae singing prophecy at Peleus's wedding.
The Charites dance at Peleus and Thetis’s wedding.
Chiron gives Peleus the Pelian ash spear later inherited and wielded by Achilles.
Later traditions say Chiron rescues or advises Peleus after Acastus betrays him.
Chiron advises Peleus how to retain Thetis despite her successive transformations.
Hestia attends the divine procession to Peleus's wedding with Thetis.
The Muses sing at Peleus's wedding to Thetis.
Tethys attends Peleus's wedding as a divine guest.
Thetis is the unwilling divine wife of the mortal hero Peleus.
Peleus holds Thetis through successive transformations and forces the marriage.
Thetis promises to make her aged mortal husband immortal.
Urania attends Peleus' wedding within the divine procession.

Pelopia.note: Pelopia is one of the competing mothers assigned to Cycnus by Ares.

Pelops.note: Clotho draws Pelops from a pure cauldron with an ivory shoulder.
Poseidon loves Pelops and carries him to Olympus.
Poseidon grants Pelops a golden chariot or horses for his race.

Pemphredo.note: Pemphredo is one of Medusa’s close Graiai kin.

Penelope.note: Circe makes Penelope immortal after Telegonus brings her to Aeaea.
Some later variants connect Hermes and Penelope as Pan's parents.
Pan is reported as the child of Penelope and Hermes.

Peneus.note: Daphne appeals to her river-god father Peneus while fleeing Apollo.
Peneus is a river son of Tethys and Oceanus.

Penia.note: Penia conceives Eros from Poros during Aphrodite's birthday feast.
Penia conceives Eros by Poros as a remedy for her lack.
Penia confronts Ploutos’ supporters, arguing that universal wealth would destroy labor.
Penia protests Ploutos’ return to Timon and defends poverty’s moral benefits.

Penthesilea.note: Penthesilea is assigned to Ares, often with Otrera as mother.

Peparethus.note: Later mythographic lists attribute Peparethus to Ariadne.
Peparethus is attributed to Dionysus and Ariadne.

Percy Jackson.note: Riordan depicts Hyperion as an armed Titan antagonist fighting Percy Jackson.

Perieres.note: Perieres is listed among the sons of Aeolus and Enarete.

Perimede.note: Perimede is listed among the daughters of Aeolus and Enarete.

Periphas.note: Tzetzes names Periphas among Aeolus' twelve intermarried children.

Periphetes.note: Apollodorus calls the club-bearing adversary of Theseus a son of Hephaestus.

Perseverance.note: Perseverance accompanies Penia’s antagonistic entourage and intimidates Ploutos.

Pertinacia.note: Roman catalogues make Obstinacy a child of Erebus and Night.

Phaea.note: A particular later mythographic genealogy assigns the Crommyonian sow to Echidna.

Phaeacians.note: Homer describes Phaeacians and Gigantes as peoples comparably close to the gods.

Phaedra.note: Aphrodite afflicts Phaedra with destructive desire for Hippolytus.
Phaedra is commonly listed as Ariadne’s sister.

Phaethon.note: Hesiodic tradition makes Phaethon Aphrodite's lover or abducted youth.
Aphrodite abducts Phaethon and appoints him keeper of her sanctuary.
This Phaethon, distinct from Helios's charioteer son, is born to Eos and Cephalus.
Later sources name a radiant horse called Phaethon among Eos's varying chariot teams.
Helios fathers Phaethon; scattered variants name other mothers.
Bound by an oath, Helios lets Phaethon drive the solar chariot.
Hemera bears Phaethon to Cephalus in a genealogy normally associated with Eos.
Philostratus imagines the Horae abandoning Olympus' gates during Phaethon's disaster.
Phaethon is Tethys's grandson through her daughter Clymene.
Tethys opens the eastern barriers for Phaethon's journey, unaware of its fatal outcome.

Phaethusa.note: Phaethusa is Helios's daughter by Neaera.
Phaethusa guards Helios's immortal livestock on Thrinacia.

Phaino.note: Phaino and Tyche belong to the company of Oceanid sisters.
Phaino and Tyche gather flowers and play among Persephone’s Oceanid companions.

Phantasos.note: Ovid names the inanimate-form dream Phantasos as Somnus’s son.
Phantasos is Morpheus’s brother and the specialist in inanimate dream-forms.
Phantasos is a dream-son specializing in inanimate forms such as stone, water, and trees.

Phaon.note: A local or later love tradition links Aphrodite with Phaon.

Phasis.note: Phasis is named among Oceanus's river sons.
Phasis is a river son of Tethys and Oceanus.

Pheraemon.note: Pheraemon is one of Aeolus' six colonizing sons.

Philammon.note: Apollo fathers Philammon in genealogies naming Chione or Leuconoe.

Philomelos.note: Later genealogies make plough-inventor Philomelos a son of Demeter.

Philomelus.note: Ploutos and Philomelus are brothers, sons of Ceres and Iasion.
Rich Ploutos refuses assistance to Philomelus, who subsequently invents improved ploughing.

Philophrosyne.note: Late Neoplatonic tradition makes Aglaea and Hephaestus parents of Philophrosyne.
Late Neoplatonic genealogy makes Philophrosyne a daughter of Hephaestus and Aglaea.

Philotes.note: Philotes and Atropos are siblings under Hesiod's Night genealogy.
Hesiod makes Philotes and Momus fatherless children of Nyx.
Philotes and Nemesis are fatherless children of Nyx.
Nyx bears Philotes without a partner.
Philotes and Thanatos belong to Nyx's fatherless brood.

Philyra.note: Philyra is Chiron's Oceanid mother and is later transformed into a linden.
Cronos unites with the Oceanid Philyra and fathers Chiron.
One form makes Cronos assume a horse’s shape during his union with Philyra.

Phineus.note: Boreas blinds Phineus in retaliation for Phineus blinding Boreas's grandsons.
Some later genealogies include Phineus among Europa’s siblings.
Medusa’s severed head petrifies Phineus when Perseus exposes it during the wedding battle.

Phineus.myth: Phineus advises noise against the island birds
Phineus.note: The prophetic adviser directs the Argonauts to repel the birds with noise.

Phlias.note: Phlias is attributed to Dionysus and Ariadne.

Phlogeus.note: Podarge is the mother of the supernatural foal Phlogeus.

Phocus.note: Nereus is Phocus' maternal grandfather through Psamathe.

Phoenice.note: Late genealogical compilations name Phoenice, daughter of Phoenix, as Proteus’ mother.

Phoenix.note: The earliest genealogy names Europa as Phoenix’s daughter.
Later harmonizing genealogies also make Phoenix Europa’s brother.
In the Agenor genealogy, Phoenix fails to recover Europa and becomes associated with Phoenicia.

Phoibe.note: Phoibe and Themis are Titan children of Gaia and Ouranos.
Themis passes Delphi’s oracle to Phoibe, who later gives it to Apollo.

Pholus.note: Pholus dies accidentally through an arrow poisoned with the Hydra's venom.

Phonoi.note: Eris bears the collective Phonoi without a named father.

Phorbas.note: Scylla is the daughter of Phorbas and Hecate.

Phorcys.note: Polyphemus is Phorcys's maternal grandson through Thoosa.
Probably Echidna’s father under the most natural reading of Hesiod.
Gaia bears Phorcys through union with Pontus.
Phorcys and Ceto beget the Graeae.
Phorcys fathers the unnamed golden-apple guardian with Ceto.
Phorcys and Nereus are sons of Pontus and Gaia.
One variant makes Phorcys and Ceto parents of the Hesperides.
Phorcys is Polyphemus’s maternal grandfather through Thoosa.
Sophocles’ lost play makes Phorcys father of two Sirens.

Phorkos.note: Scylla's father is alternatively given as Phorkos.

Phorkys.note: Phorkys is Medusa’s father in the Hesiodic marine-monster genealogy.
Scylla is the daughter of Phorkys and Hecate.
Scylla is the daughter of Phorkys and Hecate or Crataeis.
Phorkys reportedly restores Scylla after Heracles kills her.

Phthonos.note: Callimachus sends Momus to dwell with Phthonos after Apollo dismisses Envy.

Physis.note: Personified Nature places everything within Proteus or entrusts it to him.

Picolous.note: Circe fights a giant with Helios’s aid; his blood produces moly.

Picus’s companions.note: Circe changes Picus’s protesting companions into assorted beasts.

Pierides.note: Nine daughters of Pierus challenge the Muses and lose the singing contest.
The Muses transform their abusive defeated rivals into chattering magpies.
Urania joins the victorious Muses and speaks after the challengers become birds.

Pierus.note: Pierus fathers Hyacinthus with Clio in a minority genealogy.

Pirithous.note: Charon recalls ferrying Pirithous when he entered Hades to abduct Persephone.
The twins undo the abduction of Helen undertaken by Pirithous and Theseus.
Hades traps Pirithous, who commonly remains imprisoned when Heracles intervenes.

Pitys.note: After Pitys rejects him, Boreas's violence causes her death or transformation.
Pan pursues Pitys, who becomes a pine in varying late accounts.

Pleione.note: Pleione is Atlas's consort and mother of the seven Pleiades.
Pleione is named as a daughter of Tethys and Oceanus.

Plexippus.note: Boreas is variously named as Plexippus’ grandfather through Cleopatra.

Plusia.note: Plusia mothers Thelxinoe, Aoide, Arche, and Melete with Zeus.

Podarge.note: Zephyrus mates with the Harpy Podarge beside Oceanus.
Zephyrus mates with the Harpy Podarge beside Ocean; Homer does not call them married.

Podarkes.note: Aellopos bears the supernatural horse Podarkes to Boreas.

Polemos.note: Enyo is poetically called War's sister, without shared parentage specified.

Polus.note: Later harmonization tentatively equates Hyginus’s Titan Polus with Coeus, though Hyginus never explicitly does.

Polyboea.note: The Horae and associated goddesses carry Polyboea to heaven.

Polybotes.note: Poseidon battles Polybotes during the gods’ war against the Giants.
Poseidon crushes Polybotes beneath a fragment of Kos or Nisyros.

Polybus.note: Polybus, himself a son of Hermes, is named Glaucus' father.

Polydectes.note: Medusa’s severed head turns Polydectes to stone when Perseus returns.

Polydeukes.note: Polydeukes is Zeus’s son in a variable Leda genealogy.

Polydorus.note: Harmonia is the mother of the Theban dynastic heir Polydorus.

Polygonus.note: Polygonus is a son of Proteus in the Torone genealogy.

Polyhymnia.note: Polyhymnia is a daughter of Mnemosyne and Zeus.
Polyhymnia and Urania are daughters of Zeus and Mnemosyne.

Polyphonte.note: Polyphonte rejects Aphrodite and joins Artemis.

Ponos.note: Eris bears Ponos without a named father.

Poros.note: Diotima's philosophical myth makes Eros the son of Poros and Penia.
Poros fathers Eros while intoxicated with nectar at Aphrodite’s feast.
Diotima's philosophical genealogy makes Poros the son of Metis.

Porphyrion.note: Hyginus’s expanded genealogy makes Porphyrion a child of Erebus and Night.
Porphyrion is called king of the Gigantes in a distinct tradition.
Porphyrion attacks and desires Hera before Zeus and Heracles kill him.

Poseidon’s sea monster.note: Heracles kills the sea monster sent against Troy and rescues Hesione.

Potestas.note: Hyginus lists the personification Potestas among Pallas and Styx’s offspring.
Hyginus’s corrupt expanded genealogy lists Potestas among Styx’s offspring.

Pothos.note: Nonnus makes Pothos the child of Zephyrus and Iris.
Some later traditions assign Pothos to Aphrodite as a son.
Pothos appears above Europa and the bull in the marine procession.
Pothos is identified as the son of Iris and Zephyrus.
Nonnus makes Pothos the son of Zephyrus and Iris.

Priam.note: Iris conveys Zeus’s instructions and reassures Priam before his journey.
Priam.date: late eighth or early seventh BCE

Priapos.note: Aphrodite is assigned Priapos as a son, usually by Dionysus.

Prometheus the Cabeir.note: The pan-Hellenic Prometheus may have been assimilated to a distinct local Cabeiric figure.

Prophasis.note: Pindar calls the personified Excuse or Pretext a daughter of Epimetheus.

Protogeneia.note: Some traditions make Protogeneia the mother by Ares of Oxylus.

Protogonos.note: Orphic systematization assimilates Dionysus to Protogonos.
An Orphic hymn unusually calls Rhea the daughter of Protogonos.

Psamathe.note: Psamathe is a daughter of Nereus and Doris.
The Egyptian king Proteus marries the Nereid Psamathe after Aeacus.
Thetis persuades Psamathe to end her punishment of Peleus.

Pseudea.note: Eris bears the collective Pseudea without a named father.

Psyche.note: Venus persecutes Psyche and imposes four dangerous tasks.
Venus ultimately becomes Psyche's divine mother-in-law.
Psyche feeds Cerberus cakes to pass him entering and leaving the underworld.
The Gratiae diffuse balsam during Psyche’s wedding to Eros.
Charon ferries Psyche outward and back after receiving a coin each way.
Cupid becomes Psyche's hidden lover and ultimately her divinely recognized husband.
Cupid removes the underworld sleep from Psyche and revives her.
Pan counsels Psyche against suicide and urges reconciliation with Cupid.
Psyche must obtain Styx’s forbidding, deadly water as an imposed trial.
Zephyrus gently carries the exposed Psyche from a cliff into Cupid’s valley.
At Psyche’s request, Zephyrus repeatedly transports her sisters into Cupid’s valley.

Pygmalion.note: Venus answers Pygmalion's prayer by animating his ivory woman.

Pylus.note: Pylus is a son of Ares and Demonice in Apollodoran genealogy.

Pyrene.note: Pyrene is sometimes named as the mother of Cycnus by Ares.

Pyrrha.note: Pyrrha is the daughter of Epimetheus and Pandora.
Pyrrha survives Zeus’s destructive flood alongside Deucalion.

Pūṣan.note: Modern scholars propose a disputed linguistic and functional relationship between Pan and Pūṣan.

Querella.note: Roman catalogues make Complaint a child of Erebus and Night.

Rhadamanthus.note: Rhadamanthus examines, compels confession from, and punishes Tartarus’s inmates.

Rhadamanthys.note: Rhadamanthys appears beside Cronos in Pindar’s blessed western realm.
Later systems place Rhadamanthys among the judges in Hades’ realm.
Cinaethon's divergent Cretan genealogy makes Rhadamanthys Hephaestus's son.

Rhesus.note: A variant genealogy makes Euterpe the mother of Rhesus.
A competing genealogy makes Calliope the mother of Rhesus.
A competing genealogy makes Clio the mother of Rhesus.
Rhesus is a river son of Tethys and Oceanus.

Rhode.note: Later mythography names Rhode as a daughter of Amphitrite and Poseidon.
Later mythography names Rhode among Poseidon and Amphitrite’s children.

Rhodius.note: Rhodius is a river son of Tethys and Oceanus.

Rhodos.note: An individual late or local genealogy assigns Rhodos to Aphrodite.
Helios claims Rhodes and unites with its eponymous nymph.

Rhoeo.note: Rhoeo is named as Apollo's partner and mother of Anius.

Rhoiteia.note: Late and textually fragile genealogies list Rhoiteia among Proteus’ daughters.

Rhomos.note: Rhomos is a son of Circe and Odysseus and eponymous founder of Rome.

River gods.note: Dedications and reliefs associate nymphs with Cephisus, Acheloos, and local rivers.

Roma.note: Roma developed within the same civic-personification visual system as city Tyches.

Sabazios.note: Overlapping ecstatic and initiatory imagery encouraged limited identification with Sabazios.
Greek and Roman evidence identifies or compounds Zeus with Sabazios.

Sadidos.note: Sadidos is named as a son of Kronos in Philo’s Phoenician history.
The euhemerized Phoenician Kronos kills his son Sadidos.

Sagittarius.note: Later tradition sometimes identifies Chiron with Sagittarius, though ancient accounts often assign it to Crotus.

Salacia.note: Roman art and mythography identify Amphitrite with Neptune’s consort Salacia.
Roman interpretation equates Neptune’s consort Salacia with Poseidon’s Amphitrite.

Salmacis.note: Salmakis receives Hermaphroditus kindly and raises him at Halicarnassus.
Hermaphroditus resists Salmacis as she seizes and sexually assaults him.
Salmacis’ prayer causes their bodies to merge into one dual-sexed form.

Salmoneus.note: Salmoneus is listed among the sons of Aeolus and Enarete.

Samothracian Great Gods.note: Maritime cult networks sometimes associate or equate the Dioscuri with the Great Gods.

Samothracian gods.note: Glaucus appears after their invocation and orders fulfillment of vows to them.

Sangarius.note: Sangarius is a river son of Tethys and Oceanus.

Sarapis.note: Roman Egyptian magical invocations assimilate Apollo with Sarapis and other ritual powers.
Roman writers sometimes equate their overlapping healing powers, though Egyptian cult distinguishes them.
Roman Egyptian ritual combines Sarapis and Helios in composite divine invocations.

Sarpedon.note: Post-Homeric genealogy makes Sarpedon a son of Europa and Zeus.
Thanatos and Hypnos transport the dead hero's prepared body to Lycia.
Sarpedon is a heroic son of Zeus.
Zeus considers rescuing Sarpedon but permits his destined death.

Satyrs.note: Polyphemus enslaves the satyrs and forces them to tend his household.
Satyrs accompany Dionysus and search for him when separated from their god.
Nymphs and satyrs jointly accompany Dionysus in processions.

Satyrs and nymphs.note: They attend Cybele's feast with Priapus but have no direct exchange.

Scamander.note: Hephaestus boils the river with fire until Scamander submits.
Scamander is named among Oceanus's river sons.
Scamander is a river son of Tethys and Oceanus.

Scelus.note: Juno proposes summoning Discordia together with Scelus from the underworld.

Scythian “Ares”.note: Herodotus interprets the unnamed Scythian sword-god as Ares.

Semele.note: Etruscan mirrors show Semla beside Fufluns and Areatha.
Dionysus retrieves his mother from Hades and establishes her among the gods.
Harmonia is mother of Semele, later divinized as Thyone.
Hera disguises herself and induces Semele to demand Zeus's fatal divine appearance.
Spring opens the Horae's chamber and releases flowers for Semele's celebration.
The Horae attend Semele during her pregnancy with Dionysus.
Styx’s binding sanction forces Zeus to grant Semele’s fatal request.
Zeus impregnates Semele, who later demands his unveiled divine appearance.
Bound by his oath, Zeus appears in lightning and burns Semele.

Senectus.note: Roman catalogues make Old Age a child of Erebus and Night.

Septentrio.note: Some Roman wind schemes make Septentrio overlap with Boreas.

Sidon.note: The Graeco-Phoenician genealogy names Sidon or Sidonia among Pontus's children.
Sidon.date: Roman Empire; preserved early fourth century

Sileni.note: Tree-associated mountain nymphs mate with Sileni and Hermes.

Silens.note: Silens belong to Dionysus’s recurring mythic and iconographic retinue.
Nymphs and Silens jointly accompany Dionysus in processions.

Silenus.note: Polyphemus enslaves Silenus, obtains Odysseus's wine through him, and disputes over the strangers.
Silenus offers Danaë protection and marriage in sexually threatening terms.
Silenus boasts crudely of penetrating Hermaphroditus in a comic-erotic exchange.
Silenus serves Polyphemus as a slave until Odysseus defeats him.
Silenus brings the ass whose braying exposes and frustrates Priapus.

Silenus's ass.note: Priapus kills or demands sacrifice of the ass that exposed him.

Simois.note: Simois is named among Oceanus's river sons.
Simois is a river son of Tethys and Oceanus.

Sipriotes.note: Artemis transforms the Cretan boy into a girl after he sees her bathing.

Sisyphus.note: Sisyphus is listed among the sons of Aeolus and Enarete.
One variant makes Sisyphus deceive Hades and obtain temporary release.

Solymi.note: Pegasus carries Bellerophon in battle against the Solymi.

Somnus.note: Roman poets identify Hypnos with the personified Latin god Somnus.

Sophrosyne.note: Hyginus’s expanded genealogy makes Sophrosyne a child of Erebus and Night.

Sose.note: A specialized Pan is made the son of Hermes and Sose.

Sosipolis.note: Elean cult treated Sosipolis as Eileithyia's possible child or closely paired cult-child.
Sosipolis had a small shrine within or beside Tyche’s sanctuary at Elis.

Staphylus.note: Naxian tradition makes Staphylus a son of Ariadne and Dionysus.
Staphylus is attributed to Dionysus and Ariadne.

Stars.note: The stars' light participates in or derives from Aether's brilliance.
The Orphic hymn identifies the Stars as children of Night.

Sterope.note: Another tradition assigns Sterope as Oenomaus’s mother by Ares.
Sterope is one of Atlas and Pleione's seven daughters.
Sterope bears the Sirens to Achelous in the fragmentary catalogue tradition.

Steropes.note: Steropes and Crius share Gaia and Uranus as parents.
Gaia bears the Cyclops Steropes by Uranus.
Steropes is a Cyclops son of Uranus and Gaia.
Uranus conceals Steropes within Gaia; later tradition describes binding.

Sthenno.note: Sthenno is Medusa’s immortal Gorgon sister.
Sthenno pursues Perseus after he beheads Medusa.

Stheno.note: Stheno is a Gorgon sister of the Graeae.

Strymon.note: The river Strymon fathers Rhesus with Euterpe in one tradition.
Strymon is named among Oceanus's river sons.
Strymon is a river son of Tethys and Oceanus.

Stymphalos.note: Mnaseas makes Stymphalos the father of the human Stymphalides.

Syme.note: Glaucus abducts Syme, settles an island, and names it after her.

Syrinx.note: Pan pursues Syrinx; after she becomes reeds, he fashions his pipe.

Tabiti.note: Herodotus interprets the Scythian hearth goddess Tabiti as Hestia.

Tantalos.note: Tantalos is listed among Zeus’s major heroic offspring.

Taurian Parthenos.note: Greek authors and cults connected the Taurian maiden goddess with Artemis.

Tauropolis.note: Variant genealogical compilations list Tauropolis as Ariadne’s child.

Taygete.note: Taygete is one of Atlas and Pleione's seven daughters.
Taygete is listed among Zeus’s important partners.

Telchines.note: Rhea entrusts infant Poseidon to the Telchines and Capheira.
Styx water mixed with sulfur enables the Telchines to destroy living things and land.
A reported Bacchylidean variant makes four Telchines children of Tartarus and Nemesis.

Telegonus.note: A disputed cyclic notice makes Telegonus or Teledamus her son by Odysseus.
Telegonus is Circe’s son by Odysseus in cyclic and genealogical traditions.
Circe gives Telegonus the stingray-spine weapon that later kills Odysseus.
Telegonus is a son of Proteus in the Torone genealogy.

Telemachus.note: Athena mentors Telemachus in mortal disguises and prompts his search for news.
Calypso falls in love with Telemachus and offers him immortality.
Telemachus marries Circe after arriving on Aeaea with Telegonus and Penelope.
Circe makes Telemachus immortal after his arrival on Aeaea.

Telemus.myth: Telemus foretells Polyphemus’s blinding by Odysseus
Telemus.note: Polyphemus recalls Telemus’s prophecy after Odysseus reveals his identity.

Telephassa.note: Apollodorus names Telephassa as Europa’s mother.
Moschus makes Europa the daughter of Phoenix and Telephassa.

Telesphorus.note: Telesphorus is sometimes systematized as Asclepius' hooded child.
Telesphorus appears beside Asclepius as a hooded child-assistant.

Tellus.note: Roman authors translate and assimilate Greek Gaia to the Roman Earth goddess.

Telphusa.note: Telphusa deceives Apollo into rejecting her site for his sanctuary.
Apollo returns after discovering Telphusa's deception and asserts control over her site.

Tenages.note: Tenages is listed among Helios's Rhodian sons.

Tereus.note: Some genealogies make Tereus a son of Ares.

Terpsichore.note: Terpsichore is a daughter of Mnemosyne and Zeus.
Terpsichore bears the Sirens to Achelous in Apollonius’ genealogy.
Terpsichore and Urania are daughters of Zeus and Mnemosyne.

Thaicrucia.note: Late and textually fragile genealogies list Thaicrucia among Proteus’ daughters.

Thalassa.note: Ion of Chios makes Aegaeon the son of the personified Sea.
Mare is born to Aether and Dies.
Pontus and Sea generate the tribes of fishes.
The hymn addresses the Sea with language identifying or overlapping her with Tethys.

Thalia.note: Thalia is a daughter of Mnemosyne and Zeus.
Thalia and Urania are daughters of Zeus and Mnemosyne.

Thamyris.note: Thamyris boasts that he can defeat the Muses in song.
The Muses disable Thamyris, remove his voice, and erase his lyre skill.

Thasus.note: Some genealogies make Thasus Europa’s brother rather than another relative.
Thasus joins the unsuccessful search and settles the island bearing his name.

Thaumas.note: Gaia bears Thaumas through union with Pontus.
Thaumas fathers Aello and Ocypete with Electra.
Thaumas is Iris’s father in the Hesiodic genealogy.
Thaumas.date: late eighth or seventh century BCE

Thaumas.note: Thaumas and Nereus are sons of Pontus and Gaia.

The Amazons.note: Greek authors repeatedly call the Amazons daughters or descendants of Ares.

The Argonauts.note: The Sirens threaten the passing crew with their destructive song.

The Cabeiroi.note: At Zeus's order, the Cabeiroi purify Angelos in Acherusian waters.

The Fates.note: Eight cosmic Sirens sing in concert with Lachesis, Clotho, and Atropos.

The Giants.note: Hera fights the Giants in the war against Olympus.

The Hours.note: Ares sports among the Hours and other gods at Apollo’s feast.

The Moirai.note: The Moirai are invoked during Athena’s civic settlement with the Erinyes.
Eileithyia and the Fates jointly attend Evadne's delivery.
Eileithyia and the Fates jointly obstruct Alcmene's labor with crossed limbs.
The Erinyes invoke the Fates and claim linked ancient chthonic authority.
The Moirai escort Themis from Ocean to Olympus for her marriage.

The Satyrs.note: The satyrs track the cattle and investigate the strange sound of Hermes's lyre.

The Spartoi.note: Warriors spring from the teeth of Ares’s dragon, linking them to his martial lineage.

The Stars.note: The collective divine stars are offspring of Eos and Astraeus.

The Telchines.note: A fragmentary variant derives the Telchines from Pontus and Gaia.

The Thriae.note: Apollo directs Hermes toward prophetic bee-maidens whose precise identity is disputed.

The Titans.note: Hera invokes the Titans before independently producing Typhaon.

Theisoa.note: The nymph Theisoa receives and helps rear infant Poseidon.

Theoclymenus.note: The royal Proteus and Psamathe are parents of Theoclymenus.

Theoi Euergetai.note: Hestia Pantheos occupied a cultic environment associated with the deified royal couple.

Theonoe.note: Proteus fathers Eido, later called Theonoe because of her prophetic knowledge.

Theophane.note: Poseidon mates with Theophane in the golden ram’s parentage.

Thesan.note: Etruscan art adapts Greek Eos imagery, producing an artistic and interpretive equation with Thesan.

Theseus.note: Amphitrite receives Theseus and gives him a purple cloak and rose wreath.
Amphitrite gives Theseus a golden crown before his return with Minos’s ring.
Theseus attempts to carry Ariadne from Crete to Athens.
Ariadne supplies the means by which Theseus escapes the Labyrinth.
After accepting Ariadne’s aid and marriage bargain, Theseus abandons her.
A storm separates pregnant Ariadne from Theseus; she dies before his return.
Charon recalls ferrying Theseus when he entered Hades to abduct Persephone.
Theseus abandons or yields Ariadne before Dionysus takes her.
The twins invade Theseus's territory and recover Helen while he is absent.
Hades traps Theseus for entering the underworld to seize Persephone.
The Minotaur fights Theseus in the central heroic combat shown by early Greek art.
Theseus kills him by varying means, including sword or fists, and escapes.

Theseus.myth: Capture of the Bull of Minos
Theseus.note: An Archaic monument shows Theseus leading the Minotaur alive and bound instead of killing him.
Asterius becomes Theseus's friendly companion and co-champion in the game Hades.
Poseidon is Theseus’ divine father in a dual-paternity tradition.
Poseidon grants Theseus three curses, one used fatally against Hippolytus.

Thestius.note: Thestius is a son of Ares and Demonice in Apollodoran genealogy.

Thoas.note: Some lists make Thoas a son of Ariadne and Dionysus.
Clotho and the Moirai kill the Giant Thoas with bronze clubs.
Thoas is attributed to Dionysus and Ariadne.
The collective Moirai kill the Giant Thoas with bronze clubs.

Thoon.note: The Moirai collectively kill the Giant Thoon with bronze clubs.

Thoosa.note: Thoosa bears Polyphemus after union with Poseidon.
Thoosa is Polyphemus’s mother by Poseidon.
Poseidon fathers Polyphemus with the nymph Thoosa.

Thornax.note: Thornax is Iapetus's partner and mother of Buphagus.

Thracian “Ares”.note: Herodotus translates a principal Thracian god through the Greek name Ares.

Thyestes.note: Helios's reversed course defeats Thyestes's claim in the kingship contest.

Thyia.note: Thyia is one variant mother of Apollo's son Delphus.

Thymbris.note: Late genealogy names the nymph Thymbris as Pan’s mother by Hermes.

Tiresias.note: Athena blinds Tiresias after he accidentally sees her bathing.
Athena compensates Tiresias with prophecy and postmortem privileges.
Circe directs Odysseus to consult the dead prophet Tiresias.

Tisiphone.note: Latin Pavor and Terror accompany Tisiphone as she spreads madness.
Tisiphone keeps sleepless watch at the gate of Roman Tartarus.

Titaea.note: A Cretan alternative makes Titaea the mother of the Titans, including Coeus.
Cretan tradition collectively makes the Titans children of Titaea and a Curete.
Diodorus’s Atlantic genealogy makes Titaea the mother of Uranus’s children, including Hyperion.
A Cretan account makes Titaea Tethys's mother.
Diodorus's Atlantian history makes Titaea the wife of Uranus.

Titans.note: The Uranian Cyclopes and Titans are children of Gaia and Uranus.
The Titans lure, dismember, cook, and consume the child Dionysus.
Roman and later traditions often conflate Gigantes with Titans despite their distinct origins.
Hades and his brothers use the Cyclopes’ weapons to defeat the Titans.
Zeus wages a cosmic war against the Titans.
Zeus confines the defeated Titans in Tartaros.

Tithonus.note: Tithonus is Eos's mortal bedmate and enduring consort.
Eos carries beautiful young Tithonus away to the world's end.
A later variant sometimes makes Eos transform the perpetually aging Tithonus into a cicada.
Hemera inherits Eos’s partnership with Tithonus in the Memnon tradition.

Tityos.myth: Assault on the road to Pytho
Tityos.note: Tityos attacks Leto while she travels through Panopeus toward Pytho.

Tityus.note: Later versions explicitly make Apollo and Artemis shoot Leto's assailant.
Coeus calls upon Tityus during his attempted escape.

Tmolus.note: The mountain-god Tmolus judges Apollo’s music superior to Pan’s.

Torone.note: Regional genealogy makes Torone or Chrysonoe mother of Proteus’ violent sons.

Trienus.note: Scylla's uncertain father is given as Trienus, possibly a corrupted reading.

Triopas.note: Triopas is listed among Helios's Rhodian sons.

Triptolemus.note: Demeter teaches Triptolemus the Eleusinian rites.
Later tradition gives Triptolemus seed and a serpent-drawn chariot to spread agriculture.
Demeter rescues Triptolemus from rulers attempting to kill him or steal agriculture.
Triptolemus appears with Plouton, Kore, and Demeter in Eleusinian scenes.

Triteia.note: A local Achaean genealogy makes Triteia Triton’s daughter.

Trophonius.note: His consultants drink Mnemosyne’s water and later recount visions from her throne.

Tychon.note: Diodorus reports Tychon as another name for Priapus.
Strabo instead distinguishes Tychon as an Attic being resembling Priapus.

Tyndareus.note: Late resurrection catalogues name Tyndareus among those restored by Asclepius.

Typhoeus.myth: Ordered winds contrasted with Typhoeus’ destructive squalls
Typhoeus.note: Typhoeus produces ruinous squalls explicitly distinguished from Boreas, Notus, and Zephyrus.
Typhoeus fathers the Harpies in a Roman variant genealogy.

Tyro.note: Poseidon mates with Tyro and fathers Pelias and Neleus.

Tyrrhenus.note: Scylla is assigned Tyrrhenus as an alternative father.

Undines.note: Early-modern occult systems associated water elementals called undines with nymphs.

Unnamed Dreams.note: Morpheus belongs to Somnus’s unnamed multitude of one thousand dream-sons.

Upis.note: Upis is Boreas's daughter in a Hyperborean genealogy.

Vajrapāṇi.note: Gandharan art adapted Heraclean appearance for the Buddha’s protector Vajrapāṇi.

Vindonnus.note: Roman provincial worship joins Apollo with the indigenous god Vindonnus.

Virgo.note: Astraeus interprets Virgo as a celestial factor in Persephone’s horoscope.

Vis.note: Hyginus lists the personification Vis among Pallas and Styx’s offspring.
Hyginus’s corrupt expanded genealogy lists Vis among Styx’s offspring.

Voluptas.note: Cupid and Psyche become the parents of Voluptas, divine Pleasure.

Vulturnus.note: Roman wind schemes equate Eurus with Vulturnus or Volturnus.

Water.note: Chronos generates Water from his own seed.
Water generates the primordial serpent Chronos with Earth or matter.

Wisdom.note: Wisdom accompanies Penia’s antagonistic entourage and intimidates Ploutos.

Xanthos and Balios.note: Late tradition makes Giant-associated Xanthos and Balios side with the gods.

Xanthus.note: Zephyrus fathers the immortal horse Xanthus by Podarge.
The Erinyes stop the divinely speaking horse when his prophecy exceeds permitted bounds.
Podarge bears the immortal horse Xanthus to Zephyrus.
Aellopos bears a horse named Xanthus to Boreas.
Zephyrus fathers the immortal horse Xanthus upon Podarge.

Xuthus.note: Xuthus and Aeolus are sons of Hellen and Orseis.
Xuthus is one of the Liparian Aeolus' six colonizing sons.
Tzetzes names Xuthus among Aeolus' twelve intermarried children.

Zagreus.note: Later learned tradition equates Zagreus with the dismembered Orphic Dionysus.
Fragmentary Aeschylean evidence may call Zagreus Hades’ son.
The game depicts Thanatos as Zagreus's possible lover.

Zas.note: Zas and Chronos coexist eternally as ungenerated primordial beings.

Zelos.note: Ananke and Zelos jointly receive Aphrodite after her emergence.
Zelos is Nike’s sibling, born to Pallas and Styx.

Zelos.date: late eighth or early seventh century BCE

Zelos.note: Zelos is the son of Styx and Pallas.
Styx brings Zelos to Zeus, beside whom he thereafter dwells.

Zetes.note: Boreas and Oreithyia are parents of the winged Boread Zetes.
Zetes is a winged son of Boreas and Oreithyia.
Zetes chases and repels the Harpies after their attack on Phineus's meal.
One early tradition reports that Zetes and Calais kill the Harpies.
Iris stops Zetes from killing the Harpies and swears they will withdraw.

Zethos.note: Zethos is Zeus’s heroic son by Antiope.

Zeus Aktaios.note: Chiron's named cave and Zeus Aktaios' sanctuary share a seasonal Pelion ritual landscape.

Zeus Geleon.note: Zeus Geleon and Enyo shared a priesthood with Ares Enyalios.

Zeus Moiragetes.note: A lost relief represented the Moirai together with Zeus Moiragetes.

Zeus Tallaios.note: Modern scholars proposed identifying Talos with the similarly named Cretan Zeus Tallaios.

Zeus’s eagle.note: Heracles kills the eagle tormenting Prometheus.

a Curete.note: Cretan tradition collectively makes the Titans children of an unnamed Curete and Titaea.
A Cretan account makes an unnamed Curete Tethys's father.

all Olympian gods.note: The gods feast at Harmonia's wedding and bestow gifts.

chosen daimones.note: Guardian daimones lead souls onward before Atropos makes their chosen lives irreversible.

cicadas.myth: Cicadas report devotees to the Muses
cicadas.note: The transformed cicadas report to Urania which mortals honor her.

daimones.note: In Plato, Cronos appoints daimones to govern cities with peace and justice.

destructive storm winds.note: Destructive irregular winds arise from Typhoeus.

dragon guarding the Hesperides.note: A late mythographic notice calls the Hesperidean dragon the lion’s brother.

earth-born serpent.myth: A serpent assists Heracles against the lion
earth-born serpent.note: An earth-born serpent reportedly fights beside Heracles against the lion.

eni mahanahi.note: Lycian tradition adapted an indigenous divine mother within the Letoan triad.

fifty daughters.note: Selene bears fifty unnamed daughters to Endymion.

giant crab.note: Heracles kills the giant crab that assists the Hydra.

guardian daimones.note: Lachesis assigns each reincarnating soul the guardian selected through its chosen life.

lion-headed Giant.note: A figure tentatively identified as Aether grapples with a lion-headed Giant.

one of the Jupiters.note: A theologians' genealogy makes one Jupiter a son of Aether.

river gods.note: Oceanus and Tethys generate three thousand river gods.

satyrs.note: Visual groups show Hermaphroditus resisting pursuit, seizure, or assault by satyrs.

the Argonauts.note: Proteus emerges from Pharos and directs the Argonauts toward Lemnos.

the Argonauts.myth: The Argonauts repel the birds of Ares
the Argonauts.note: The Argonauts use shields, spears, shouting, and noise to drive them away.

the Argonauts.myth: Talos prevents the Argonauts landing on Crete
the Argonauts.note: Talos tears rocks from the cliffs and hurls them at the approaching Argonauts.
Triton reveals the outlet and physically guides the Argo from the lake.

the Cabeiri.note: Proteus is maternal grandfather of the three Cabeiri through Cabeiro.

the Cabeirian nymphs.note: Proteus is maternal grandfather of three Cabeirian nymphs through Cabeiro.

the Cephallenians.note: A damaged fragment may make Calypso and Hermes progenitors of the Cephallenians.

the Colchian dragon.note: Invoked by Medea, Somnus overcomes the dragon guarding the Golden Fleece.

the Curetes.note: A Cretan alternative makes one Curete the father of the Titans.

the Dreams.note: The Dreams and Atropos are siblings under Hesiod's Night genealogy.
Hesiod makes the Dreams and Momus fatherless children of Nyx.

the Erotes.note: Nonnus describes Hypnos as a servant or attendant of the Loves.

the Giants.note: An inscribed Asteria fights among the gods against the Giants.
Pergamene sculpture places Nereus among combatants, without identifying his opponent.

the Gorgons.note: The Graeae rotate the shared eye while guarding the Gorgons.

the Heliadai.note: Helios fathers seven Rhodian sons with Rhodos.

the Heliades.note: Developed Phaethon traditions make the mourning Heliades Helios's daughters.

the Hesperides.myth: Atlas bears heaven beside the Hesperides
the Hesperides.note: Atlas stands before the Hesperides at the world's western limit.
Diodorus makes the seven Hesperides daughters of Atlas and Hesperis.
The Hesperides give Atlas the apples that he carries to Heracles.
The Hesperides and Atropos are siblings under Hesiod's Night genealogy.
A South Italian vase assimilates a Calypso to the western Hesperides.
The Hesperides are Lachesis's siblings under Hesiod's genealogy from Nyx.
Hesiod makes the Hesperides and Momus fatherless children of Nyx.
The Hesperides and Nemesis are fatherless children of Nyx.
The Hesperides and Thanatos belong to Nyx's fatherless brood.

the Hours.note: The Hours tend, harness, or surround Helios's chariot.
Zephyrus delivers Aphrodite, whom the Hours then receive, clothe, and adorn.

the Hundred-Handers.note: The Hundred-Handers help Zeus defeat and confine the Titans, including Coeus by inference.

the Hydra.note: A possibly Tartarean Hydra joins in barring Coeus’s ascent.

the Moirai.note: The three-formed Moirai are called helmsmen who steer Necessity.
Hesiod makes the Moirai and Momus fatherless children of Nyx.
The Moirai and Nemesis are fatherless children of Nyx.
The Moirai and Thanatos belong to Nyx's brood.
The Moirai trick Typhon into eating fruits that weaken him.

the Molionids.note: The human Stymphalides welcome the Molionids while refusing Heracles hospitality.

the Oceanids.note: Metis belongs to the collective of Oceanus and Tethys's daughters.

the Olympian gods.note: A late commentary reports that Astraeus took arms against the gods.
Hebe pours nectar for the assembled Olympian gods.
Styx’s water sanctions their oaths and disables and excludes divine perjurers for ten years.
Typhon terrifies the Olympians into fleeing and assuming animal forms.

the Pleiades.note: The Pleiades are collectively identified as Atlas's daughters.

the Rivers.note: Tyche and the Rivers collectively share responsibility for nurturing youths.

the Stars.note: Astraeus and Eos collectively parent the stars crowning heaven.

the Telchines.note: Conflicting Rhodian sources associate the Telchines with raising Poseidon.
Conflicting late traditions connect Poseidon genealogically with the Telchines.

the Titans.note: Aether and Terra generate the Titans.
Atlas commands the Titans in Hyginus's renewed revolt against Jupiter.
The Titans share Gaia and Uranus as parents with the Hundred-Handers.
The brothers bombard, overwhelm, bind, and consign the Titans to Tartarus.
The brothers guard the defeated Titans after the Olympian victory.
In a competing tradition, Aegaeon fights as an ally of the Titans.
the Titans.date: late seventh century BCE or later

the Titans.note: The defeated Titans are bound beneath the earth in Tartarus.

the ass.note: An ass challenges Priapus over genital size or prowess; Priapus wins.
Priapus kills the ass after defeating it in their sexual contest.

the birds.note: The birds arise as offspring of Eros's union with Chaos.
Eros and Chaos generate the primordial race of birds.

the generating goddess of Parmenides.note: The cosmological goddess devises Eros first among all the gods.

the gods.note: The gods select Ganymede for his beauty and carry him away.
Ganymede serves nectar to the assembled gods after his translation.
Homeric language possibly makes Oceanus and mother Tethys divine progenitors, though the grammar is debated.

the gods below.note: Hera calls the underworld gods as witnesses alongside Styx.

the race of birds.note: The primordial race of birds arises from Eros's union with Chaos.

the river gods.note: Metis shares Oceanus and Tethys as parents with the river gods.
Tethys bears three thousand river sons to Oceanus.

the satyrs.note: Satyrs help haul Danaë and infant Perseus ashore in a net.
The satyrs serve him unwillingly and join Odysseus after his blinding.

the serpent guarding the golden apples.note: Broader Phorcyd genealogy can make the golden-apples serpent their sibling.

the stars.note: The stars and Boreas are offspring of Eos and Astraeus.
Notus and the stars share Eos and Astraeus as parents.
The stars share Eos and Astraeus as parents with Zephyrus.

the unnamed equipment-bearing nymphs.note: The Graeae know and reveal their location; no meeting is narrated.
